title: TFOS Lifestyle: Impact of lifestyle challenges on the ocular surface
article_subtype: Narrative review incorporating a systematic review and meta-analysis of chronic primary pain disorders and dry eye disease
condition_or_topic: Lifestyle challenges and dry eye disease (DED) and other ocular surface diseases
clinical_background: DED has multiple manifestations, and its symptoms do not always correspond to measurable ocular surface signs. Mental, physical, and social factors have been linked to different aspects of DED and other ocular surface diseases, but many reported relationships come from cross-sectional studies. Distinguishing symptoms, tear-film and ocular surface abnormalities, and DED subtypes is important when examining these associations.
objectives: Review evidence on associations and possible mechanisms linking contemporary lifestyle challenges with DED and other ocular surface diseases, with attention to mental health, physical factors, and social factors.
Within the review, systematically identify, appraise, and synthesize studies evaluating DED in people with chronic primary pain disorders.
clinical_question: For the embedded systematic review: In adults with chronic primary pain disorders (population and exposure), compared with adults without those disorders from the same studies (comparator), what are the odds of DED (outcome)?
study_design: A narrative review based on a non-systematic search, with an embedded systematic review and meta-analysis of observational evidence on chronic primary pain disorders and dry eye disease (DED). The systematic review followed a prespecified protocol registered as CRD42021296994 and was reported in accordance with PRISMA 2.

population.description: For the embedded systematic review, adults aged 18 years and over with a primary pain disorder were compared with controls from the same study. Primary pain disorders involved pain in one or more anatomical regions that persisted or recurred for longer than 3 months and was not better explained by another diagnosis.
inclusion_criteria: Published systematic reviews and observational case-control, cohort, cross-sectional, or epidemiological studies, whether retrospective or prospective.
Studies in English that evaluated DED in adults with a primary pain disorder and included a control population from the same study.
Studies identifying pain disorders through clinical diagnostic criteria, clinician assessment, International Classification of Diseases codes, or participant self-report.
Studies identifying DED through symptoms and/or signs, participant self-report of a diagnosis, or International Classification of Diseases codes.
exclusion_criteria: Conference abstracts, case reports, case series, preclinical studies, and non-systematic reviews.
Populations with secondary pain attributable to another cause, such as diabetic neuropathy or post-surgical or post-traumatic pain.

comparators: Participants without the primary pain disorder being evaluated, drawn from the same study.

primary: Odds of DED in people with a chronic primary pain disorder relative to controls, expressed as an OR with 95% CIs.

statistical_methods: For the narrative review, authors searched MEDLINE and Google Scholar non-systematically, selected relevant publications, and prioritized studies with stronger methods when several addressed the same topic. The embedded systematic review searched Ovid Medline and Ovid Embase from inception to 9 December 2021, supplemented by reference-list searches. Two reviewers independently screened records, extracted data, and assessed risk of bias, resolving disagreements by consensus. Adjusted ORs were extracted where possible. When at least three studies provided outcomes for the same pain disorder, ORs and 95% CIs were pooled using a random-effects inverse variance model; reported ORs and their 95% CIs were log-transformed, and dichotomous case data were converted to ORs when needed. Clinical and methodological differences were examined, and statistical heterogeneity was assessed with forest plots, I2, and τ2; an I2 of 60% or more was considered consistent with moderate heterogeneity. Where there were more than ten studies, a prediction interval was presented. Sensitivity analyses for heterogeneity >60% excluded studies that did not diagnose DED through clinical assessment of symptoms or signs, provided at least three studies remained. Planned analyses by aqueous deficient or evaporative DED subtype could not be performed because too few studies reported subtype data. For meta-analyses with at least 10 studies, potential publication bias was assessed by visual inspection of a funnel plot. Analyses used R Project for Statistical Computing.
quality_assessment_tool: AMSTAR-2 for systematic reviews; Newcastle-Ottawa scale for observational studies; Grading of Recommendations, Assessment, Development and Evaluation (GRADE) for certainty of evidence.
interpretation: The report links mental, physical and social factors with different manifestations of dry eye disease (DED) and other ocular surface disorders. Associations with depression, anxiety, stress and sleep disturbance are generally stronger for DED symptoms than for clinical signs. Obesity has been linked to meibomian gland and eyelid abnormalities, while face mask wear may worsen DED, particularly its evaporative features. In the report’s systematic review, the pooled odds of DED were higher among people with migraine (OR 1.61, 95% CI 1.39–1.87), fibromyalgia (OR 1.91, 95% CI 1.63–2.24), irritable bowel syndrome (OR 2.16, 95% CI 1.65–2.82) and back pain (OR 1.60, 95% CI 1.39–1.83) than among people without the corresponding condition. Substantial heterogeneity and low or very low certainty prevent a precise conclusion about the strength of these associations. Evidence that smoking itself is associated with DED remains inconclusive, although smoke exposure affects the tear film and ocular surface. Clinical evidence concerning cannabis and many other recreational drugs is limited.
comparison_with_prior_evidence: The report’s findings on mental health and sleep broadly agree with the observational studies it reviews, which more consistently associate these factors with DED symptoms than signs. The review by Chen et al. also reported higher odds of DED in migraine, but the report judges that review to have methodological problems that may compromise its findings. Its discussion of obesity and tobacco notes conflicting population-based and clinical findings. Unlike human sleep studies, which have not established a strong association with DED signs, the cited sleep-deprivation experiments in mice produced ocular surface changes and reduced tear secretion. Findings from cited studies of treatments for DED and associated psychological or sleep symptoms are not uniform and do not establish that improving one condition will reliably improve the other.
clinical_implications: Psychological conditions, sleep disturbance and pain outside the eye may help explain severe DED symptoms when ocular surface signs are comparatively limited; the mechanisms remain uncertain.
Sleep disorders and psychological disturbances may be difficult to disentangle in people with DED, so their co-occurrence matters when interpreting symptoms.
Airflow from continuous positive airway pressure devices and prolonged face mask wear may aggravate ocular surface symptoms; pre-existing DED may increase susceptibility to effects of mask wear.
Sexual and reproductive concerns can coexist with conditions associated with DED and affect quality of life, but many of the relationships and mechanisms remain poorly understood.
Smoke exposure, including passive exposure, may contribute to tear film instability even though the association between smoking status and a DED diagnosis is unresolved.
practice_implications: Carefully screen patients with migraine, fibromyalgia, irritable bowel syndrome or back pain for DED, while recognizing the low or very low certainty of the estimated associations.
Consider an underlying anxiety disorder and the patient’s ability to cope with anxiety when assessing DED.
In a DED clinic, address both sleep disorders and psychological disturbances rather than focusing exclusively on either condition.

For users of continuous positive airway pressure devices, give attention to patient-specific mask fit and teach appropriate fitting and nighttime artificial tear or topical emollient use to help limit ocular surface effects.
Discuss smoking and its potential effects on the tear film and ocular surface with patients; the report does not establish that cessation improves ocular surface health.

For problematic eye rubbing, consider underlying ocular disease, explain potential consequences and triggers, and emphasize lid hygiene, ocular surface care and avoidance of allergens or chemical irritants. Consider cognitive behavioral therapy when persistent rubbing poses a risk of long-term damage, and consider assessment for psychiatric disease when tissue-damaging rubbing appears psychogenic.
Consider screening and treatment for ocular disorders that may provoke rubbing, including ocular dryness, corneal deformation, anterior blepharitis and meibomian gland dysfunction.

Follow the cited literature review’s recommendation for routine gynecological consultation after hematopoietic stem cell transplantation, including for asymptomatic women, to permit early recognition and preventive therapy when needed.
limitations: The narrative review used a non-systematic search and selected relevant literature rather than attempting exhaustive coverage.

Most reported lifestyle associations come from cross-sectional studies, so their direction and causality cannot be established; confounding by comorbid conditions and medication use remains important.
Definitions and assessments of DED, pain disorders and other exposures differ across studies, limiting comparisons and contributing to heterogeneity.

In the chronic pain systematic review, certainty was very low for migraine, fibromyalgia and back pain and low for irritable bowel syndrome. Risk of bias, particularly in participant selection and disease classification, limits confidence and generalizability.

Too few studies reported aqueous deficient or evaporative DED separately to support the planned subtype analysis. Too few used a DED definition combining symptoms and signs to permit a pooled estimate restricted to that definition.
Few studies in the chronic pain review reported concomitant medication use, leaving its possible contribution unresolved.

Evidence on anxiety and DED frequently comes from veteran populations, limiting its established generalizability. Clinical studies of cannabis and other recreational drugs are scarce, with much of the latter literature consisting of case reports or case series.
Evidence about the ocular surface effects of smoking cessation is minimal, and studies of interventions directed at sleep or stress do not establish their effects on DED.
open_questions: Whether mental health conditions cause or follow changes in DED symptoms, and how much medication use, pain and sleep contribute to the observed associations.
Whether treating DED changes depression, anxiety, stress or sleep outcomes, and whether treating those conditions changes DED outcomes.
Which DED phenotypes and signs are most closely associated with chronic pain, and whether pain severity changes the likelihood or severity of DED.
Whether obesity-related ocular findings are attributable to obesity itself, associated conditions such as sleep apnea, or their treatment.
Whether smoking status is independently associated with DED and whether smoking cessation improves ocular surface health.
What effects cannabis and other recreational drugs have on DED and the ocular surface in clinical populations.
future_directions: Conduct longitudinal and interventional studies of lifestyle factors and ocular surface outcomes that account for relevant comorbidities, medications and the multifactorial nature of DED.
Use clearer, more consistent diagnostic criteria for pain conditions and DED, assess both DED symptoms and signs, distinguish aqueous deficient from evaporative DED, and standardize pain measurement.
Test sleep-directed and DED-directed interventions in randomized studies while monitoring psychological symptoms and pain as potential covariates.

Investigate molecular, neural, inflammatory and hormonal mechanisms through clinical, mechanistic and animal studies, including pathways involving brain-derived neurotrophic factor and peroxisome proliferator-activated receptors.
Study how treatment of psychological distress, coping and resilience affects DED, and clarify the contribution and timing of antidepressant exposure.
Investigate ocular surface signs and DED subtypes in chronic pain populations, including the possible contribution of medications used for pain conditions.

Evaluate preventive and therapeutic approaches for sexual and reproductive issues associated with ocular surface disease, and clarify their epidemiological, functional, neural, immune and psychosocial relationships.
Examine the ocular surface effects of smoking cessation and other modifiable exposures, and undertake higher-quality clinical studies of cannabis and other recreational drugs.

main_conclusion: Mental, physical, and social factors are associated with DED manifestations and other ocular surface conditions, although most evidence is cross-sectional. The authors call for longitudinal research that accounts for confounding and the multifactorial nature of DED, alongside mechanistic studies.
narrative_summary:
This TFOS Lifestyle review examined associations between contemporary lifestyle challenges and DED or other ocular surface diseases. Its narrative component used a non-systematic search of MEDLINE and Google Scholar; an embedded, prospectively registered systematic review evaluated chronic primary pain disorders. Across populations, depression, anxiety, and stress were more consistently associated with DED symptoms than with clinical signs. Sleep quality and duration were also linked to DED symptoms, although psychological comorbidity may influence that relationship. Obesity was linked to meibomian gland and eyelid abnormalities, and face-mask wear emerged as a possible contributor to evaporative DED. Findings concerning smoking and DED diagnosis were inconclusive, despite evidence of tear-film disturbance; cocaine was associated with reduced corneal sensitivity, while alcohol consumption was linked to tear-film changes and symptoms.

The embedded meta-analysis found higher odds of DED in people with migraine (1.61, 95% CI 1.39–1.87), fibromyalgia (1.91, 95% CI 1.63–2.24), irritable bowel syndrome (2.16, 95% CI 1.65–2.82), and back pain (1.60, 95% CI 1.39–1.83). Certainty was low or very low, and heterogeneity limited precision. The authors advise careful DED screening in patients with these pain conditions. They also emphasize assessing symptoms and signs separately and pursuing longitudinal studies that address confounders, diagnostic differences, and DED subtype.

main_findings.description: The report's meta-analysis found higher odds of DED among people with migraine than among people without migraine.
main_findings.context: Pooled analysis of 11 studies; I2 = 88%; prediction interval 0.98 to 2.65. The prediction interval allows for no association in future studies. GRADE certainty was very low.

main_findings.description: The report's meta-analysis found higher odds of DED among people with fibromyalgia than among those without fibromyalgia.
main_findings.context: Pooled analysis of six studies; I2 = 84% in the effects summary, while Table 5 reports 81% for the main analysis. GRADE certainty was very low.

main_findings.description: The report's meta-analysis found higher odds of DED among people with irritable bowel syndrome than among those without it.
main_findings.context: Pooled analysis of five studies; I2 = 85%. Individual-study effects pointed in the same direction. GRADE certainty was low.

main_findings.description: The report's meta-analysis found higher odds of DED among people with back pain than among those without back pain.
main_findings.context: Pooled analysis of three studies; I2 = 63%. Individual-study effects pointed in the same direction. GRADE certainty was very low.

subgroup_analyses: The chronic-pain review identified 23 eligible studies after screening 1417 records following duplicate removal from 1570 search records: one systematic review and 22 observational studies. The reported observational designs comprised 16 prospective cross-sectional studies, two retrospective case-control studies and three retrospective chart reviews.

The chronic-pain review found a cited systematic review to be of critically low quality, with high risk of bias in eight of the 16 AMSTAR-2 domains. Among the 22 observational studies, seven received seven out of nine Newcastle-Ottawa stars and the lowest score was four out of nine; 16 studies received fewer than two of four stars for participant selection.

In the chronic-pain review, 11 of 22 observational studies assessed both DED symptoms and signs, five assessed symptoms only, one assessed signs only and five used disease coding. Only one applied 2017 TFOS DEWS II criteria. The report could not analyse aqueous-deficient versus evaporative DED subtypes because too few studies supplied subtype data.

The chronic-pain review's sensitivity analyses, restricted to clinical symptom or sign assessments, yielded OR 1.42 (95% CI 1.17–1.72; I2 = 36%; 5 studies) for migraine, OR 2.21 (95% CI 2.03–2.41; I2 = 0%; 3 studies) for fibromyalgia and OR 2.89 (95% CI 1.50–5.54; I2 = 79%; 3 studies) for irritable bowel syndrome. Too few studies permitted the corresponding back-pain analysis.
A funnel plot for the migraine synthesis suggested possible publication bias because small studies reporting weaker associations were relatively scarce.

In a Korean survey, both a DED diagnosis (OR 1.32; 95% CI 1.11–1.57) and DED symptoms (OR 1.5, 95% CI 1.30–1.73) were associated with depression. Across the studies discussed, associations with psychological conditions generally involved DED symptoms more consistently than clinical signs.
In 657 Korean elders, the depression–DED symptom association differed by tear production: Schirmer>5 mm, OR 3.08 (95% CI 1.93–4.93; p < 0.001); Schirmer<5 mm, OR 1.52 (95% CI 0.70–3.30; p = 0.29).

In South Florida veterans, adjusted associations with a DED diagnosis persisted for post-traumatic stress disorder (OR 1.40, 95% CI 1.22–1.60, p < 0.0001) and major depressive disorder (OR 1.31, 95% CI 1.14–1.50, p < 0.0001). The report cautions that veteran findings require assessment in other populations.

A Korean study found that, among men diagnosed with DED, those with symptoms reported more stress (28.7% vs. 24.0%, p = 0.03), depression (9.3% vs. 6.1%, p = 0.003) and suicidal ideation (12.0% vs. 9.0%, p = 0.04) than those without symptoms. The corresponding comparisons among women were stress 35.7% vs. 28.1%, depression 23.2% vs. 17.5%, and suicidal ideation 22.0% vs. 16.6%, all p < 0.001.

In New Zealand residents, better self-perceived health was associated with lower odds of aqueous tear deficiency (OR 0.54, 95% CI 0.34–0.85) and meibomian gland dysfunction (OR 0.63, 95% CI 0.45–0.88); greater psychological stress was associated with higher odds of aqueous tear deficiency (OR 2.28, 95% CI 1.14–4.49) and MGD (OR 1.87, 95% CI 1.20–2.89).

In a Japanese sleep survey, comparing the greatest with the least difficulty falling asleep yielded adjusted DED ORs of 2.23 (95% CI 1.99–2.49) for men and 1.91 (95% CI 1.76–2.07) for women. Associations were stronger for severe DED symptoms than for clinically diagnosed DED.

A Korean study of 4185 older adults associated sleep duration ≥9 h/day with lower odds of DED symptoms (adjusted OR 0.52, 95% CI 0.33 0.83). In a Netherlands study, 44.9% of participants with highly symptomatic DED had poor sleep quality.

In a Japanese body-mass-index survey, the adjusted DED OR per kg/m2 increment was 0.98 (95% CI 0.97–0.99) for men and 0.97 (95% CI 0.97–0.98) for women. By contrast, an Australian clinic study found a significant relationship between body fat percentage and symptom scores in women but not men.

In a face-mask study of 66 patients with DED and 62 controls, consistent wear for 3 months worsened tear breakup time and ocular surface staining in both groups, more markedly among patients with DED; changes were particularly evident with wear exceeding 6 h per day.

In a Netherlands tobacco cohort, current smoking was associated with lower DED risk than never smoking (adjusted OR 0.87, 95% CI 0.80–0.94), whereas former smoking was associated with higher risk (adjusted OR 1.09, 95% CI 1.03–1.15). The report regards the overall smoking–DED association as inconclusive.
In a Dutch study, alcohol consumption was associated with DED among women but not men.
secondary_results: A cited prevalence synthesis found depression in 25% of people with eye diseases (1502/6589; 95% CI 0.20–0.30); the estimate for DED was 29% (95% CI 0.17–0.40). A separate cited meta-analysis estimated depression prevalence among patients with DED at 40% (95% CI 0.29–0.52).

Among 472 Shanghai patients seeking care for depression and/or anxiety, 81% reported at least one DED symptom and 60% had both a symptom and a sign. DED was associated with longer psychiatric-disorder duration (54 ± 59 versus 39 ± 39 months), longer antianxiety or antidepressant use (17 ± 25 versus 10 ± 18 months), and selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor use after age and sex adjustment.

A Hungarian study correlated Ocular Surface Disease Index and Shortened Beck Depression Inventory scores at r = 0.31 (p < 0.01). In a Beijing study of 1957 people, depression scores correlated weakly with DED symptoms (r = 0.07; p = 0.01), but not tear breakup time (p = 0.18), Schirmer score (p = 0.37), corneal staining (p = 0.30) or meibomian gland dysfunction (p = 0.93).

A German study reported a higher mean Beck Depression Inventory score in participants with DED (11.95 ± 8.46; p < 0.0001 versus controls), without a correlation between depression severity and DED symptom or sign severity.

A Turkish comparison reported Schirmer scores of 7.24 ± 6.02, 6.58 ± 4.9 and 18.79 ± 4.9 mm wetting in newly diagnosed depression, anxiety and controls, respectively (p < 0.05). Corresponding tear breakup times were 5.6 ± 3.5, 5.62 ± 3.1 and 13.37 ± 1.7 s (p < 0.05), and Oxford scale scores were 1.9 ± 0.7, 2.1 ± 0.6 and 0.7 ± 0.4 (p < 0.001).

One study found higher tear interleukin-6, interleukin-17 and tumor necrosis factor-α in 32 antidepressant-treated people with depression than in 34 controls (all p < 0.001); a larger multicentre study (n = 535) did not replicate differences in inflammatory markers by depression status. Another comparison found higher tear matrix metalloproteinase 9 (MMP-9) in depression (n = 10) than in controls (n = 21).

A comparison of treated depression or anxiety with controls found tear breakup time of 7.05 ± 4.86 versus 12.53 ± 4.75 s, Oxford staining of 0.78 ± 0.76 versus 0.11 ± 0.32, and Ocular Surface Disease Index scores of 32.07 ± 19.08 versus 16.31 ± 14.28, respectively (p < 0.001 for each). Both groups' tear breakup and staining values remained within normal ranges, making their clinical significance uncertain.

Among patients newly taking an antidepressant, mean Schirmer scores were 10.4 ± 5.8 versus 12.3 ± 0.7 mm wetting in 54 treated patients and 57 controls. A Schirmer score<5 mm wetting occurred in 35% using a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor versus 18.8% using a serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor. Conversely, a Netherlands population study (n = 79,606) found no association between DED symptoms and major antidepressant classes after adjustment; among patients with depression, selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor use was associated with lower DED risk (OR 0.87, 95% CI 0.77–0.98).
In a secondary analysis of a randomized trial, DED symptoms and signs improved over time in both omega 3 and placebo groups, while depressive symptoms remained unchanged.

Among 136 South Florida veterans, correlations of 5-item Dry Eye Questionnaire and Ocular Surface Disease Index scores with Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder Checklist: Military Version scores were r = 0.45 and 0.58, respectively (p < 0.05); correlations with Patient Health Questionnaire-9 scores were r = 0.42 and 0.55 (p < 0.05).

Among 248 veterans, 5-item Dry Eye Questionnaire scores were 13.4 ± 1.1 with post-traumatic stress disorder, 12.0 ± 0.8 with depression and 9.8 ± 0.4 without either condition (p < 0.01 and p = 0.02, respectively, versus neither). Multivariable analyses associated symptom severity with post-traumatic stress disorder diagnosis (OR 4.08, p = 0.04) and selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor use (OR 2.66, p = 0.05); DED signs did not differ significantly across the three groups.

In 326 veterans, anxiety, post-traumatic stress disorder and depression scores correlated with a DED phenotype in which symptoms outweighed signs: r = 0.41 (p < 0.005), r = 0.46 (p < 0.0005) and r = 0.41 (p < 0.0005), respectively.

In a study of 233 participants, 5-item Dry Eye Questionnaire scores correlated with burning (r = 0.37), wind sensitivity (r = 0.37) and light sensitivity (r = 0.34), all p < 0.001; they also correlated with anxiety (r = 0.21, p = 0.001) and depression (r = 0.34, p < 0.001).

In a Turkish anxiety study, Schirmer values were 7.24 ± 6.02 versus 18.79 ± 4.9 mm wetting, tear breakup times 5.62 ± 3.1 versus 13.37 ± 1.7 s, and Oxford scale staining 1.9 ± 0.7 versus 0.7 ± 0.4 in 35 newly diagnosed patients versus 37 controls (p < 0.001 for each comparison).

After individualized DED treatment in 45 clinic patients, the average Dry Eye Management Scale score changed from 5.8 ± 1.8 to 4.6 ± 2.2 (p = 0.01) and the average 7-item Generalized Anxiety Disorder scale score from 5.6 ± 5.5 to 3.3 ± 4.6 (p = 0.05); mean follow-up was 13.8 ± 4.9 weeks.

Among 194 veterans, Pain Catastrophizing Scale scores correlated with 5-item Dry Eye Questionnaire scores (r = 0.41, p < 0.0005), Ocular Surface Disease Index scores (r = 0.49, p < 0.0005), numeric ocular-pain ratings (r = 0.48, p < 0.0005) and Neuropathic Pain Symptom Inventory-Eye scores (r = 0.48, p < 0.0005). Tear parameters were not associated with catastrophizing intensity.

In 211 young adults, Ocular Surface Disease Index scores correlated with dry-eye quality-of-life (r = 0.67), anxiety (r = 0.45), depression (r = 0.54) and stress (r = 0.44) scores, all p < 0.001. Most ocular signs were not significantly associated with the psychological subscales.

In the China Hangzhou sleep study, poorer subjective sleep quality, longer latency, shorter duration, lower efficiency, sleep disturbance and daytime dysfunction were associated with greater DED symptom severity after accounting for potential confounders. Table 1 gives PSQI-associated odds ratios of 1.07, 1.13 and 1.14 for mild, moderate and severe DED, respectively (all p < 0.001).

A Japanese clinic study reported Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index scores of 6.4 ± 3.2 in severe DED (n = 146) versus 5.5 ± 3.3 in mild DED (n = 155), without healthy controls. Among US veterans, at least moderate insomnia occurred in 61% of a high-ocular-pain group, 41% of a low-ocular-pain group and 18% of controls (p < 0.0005 for all).

In a mouse sleep-deprivation model, ocular epithelial disruption, lipid accumulation, altered microvilli and reduced tear production appeared after 10 days; resting for 14 days reversed the observed changes. In an experiment involving 20 healthy males, the sleep-deprived group had higher tear osmolarity, shorter tear breakup time and lower tear secretion than controls at 6 a.m.

In 40 men grouped by body mass index, mean non-invasive tear breakup time was 8.5 versus 14.7 s for elevated versus normal body mass index (p < 0.05). Tear meniscus height and phenol red thread scores did not differ significantly.

Among 350,420 continuous positive airway pressure device users, DED prevalence over 36 months was 13.0%, compared with 6.7% in the general US population. Among 40 people initiating device use, ocular irritation increased from 42.5% before use to 57.5% afterward (p = 0.031).

After eye rubbing for 2 min, tear breakup time in 49 healthy people decreased from 15.3 to 13.9 s (p = 0.0001); the non-rubbed contralateral eye changed from 15.3 to 14.8 s without a significant difference (p = 0.096).

In a study comparing complete androgen insensitivity syndrome with controls, DED symptoms were reported by 78% versus 14%; tear meniscus abnormalities and meibomian gland dysfunction were also more frequent in the syndrome group.

In a study of 117 women undergoing assisted reproduction, a Schirmer test result <10 mm in at least one eye became more frequent in the third trimester (p = 0.02) and three months post-partum (p = 0.04); other phases were comparable with baseline (p > 0.05).

In a pregnancy treatment study of 4808 individuals, congenital-abnormality rates were 14.9% among 936 exposed to sodium hyaluronate 0.1% versus 12.3% among unexposed women. The report describes conventional artificial tears as safe in pregnancy and reports similar findings for diquafosol and 0.3% sodium hyaluronate.

A Netherlands cross-sectional study of 425 patients with DED found at least one chronic pain syndrome in 17%. Pain syndromes were associated with worse DED symptoms, but not worse signs; those with pain had less corneal staining and higher Schirmer scores.

A Taiwanese fibromyalgia study reported DED incidence of 7.37/10,000 in 25,777 people with fibromyalgia versus 4.81/ 10,000 in 103,108 controls. After adjustment, DED odds were 1.39-fold higher for men and 1.45-fold higher for women with fibromyalgia.

In a Turkish migraine comparison, mean Ocular Surface Disease Index scores were 45.21 versus 26.59 (p = 0.001), Schirmer scores 14.39 versus 21.63 mm wetting (p = 0.001), and tear breakup times 9.54 versus 14.96 s (p = 0.001) for migraine versus control groups; mean signs in both groups were near normal limits.

In the chronic-pain review, studies not providing dichotomous DED outcomes could not enter the relevant meta-analyses. Gallar et al. reported DED symptoms in 18 of 20 participants with fibromyalgia versus none of 18 controls; Erkan Turan et al. found worse symptom, tear-breakup and staining measures in fibromyalgia without an intergroup Schirmer difference. Uçar et al. found higher Ocular Surface Disease Index scores (p = 0.008) and shorter tear breakup time in irritable bowel syndrome.

Studies comparing smokers with non-smokers generally reported shorter tear breakup time; findings for symptoms and tear production varied. A study of 33 waterpipe smokers and 31 non-smokers found higher osmolarity and corneal staining and shorter tear breakup time in smokers, without an Ocular Surface Disease Index difference.

In a prospective study of 112 children with ocular discomfort, 80 (71%) met DED criteria. Daily cigarette exposure and exposure duration were 17.70 ± 14.19 and 10.00 ± 3.77 h among children with DED versus 0.65 ± 2.55 and 0.70 ± 2.38 h without DED (p < 0.0001 for both).

A cited pterygium review found a lower risk among cigarette smokers, whereas other studies reported no association or increased risk. A Singapore cohort reported OR 0.41 (95% CI 0.16–0.87) for current smoking; a Southern Harbin study reported OR 1.90 (95% CI 1.51–2.35; p = 0.001) among smokers.

A study of habitual cocaine use found reduced corneal sensitivity in 26 cocaine users but no heroin users, with 6 cases of neurotrophic keratitis among cocaine users. In another study, tear production decreased while under cocaine's effects in 17 of 22 eyes, by an average 16.52 ± 10.13 mm (range 1–38 mm; p = 0.0024).

A systematic review of 11 crack cocaine case reports found bilateral involvement in 63%, corneal infection in 83% and substantial visual impairment in the affected eye in 22%. A series of 3 users of the synthetic opioid MT-45 reported DED along with hair and skin effects.

Clinical evidence on cannabis and DED was considered insufficient. A comparison of 28 people with cannabinoid use disorder and 32 controls reported corneal endothelial density of 2900 ± 211 versus 3097 ± 214 cells/mm2 (p < 0.01).

Studies cited on alcohol reported tear-film deterioration, reduced tear volume, and ethanol in tears associated with increased osmolarity and worse DED symptoms. A prospective observational study reported correlations between caffeine intake during the ovulatory phase and both tear breakup time (r = 0.5, p = 0.02) and phenol red thread values (r = 0.5, p = 0.01).

document_sections.heading: A B S T R A C T
document_sections.content: Mental, physical, and social factors have been associated with ocular surface diseases, particularly dry eye disease (DED). Cross-sectional studies link depression, anxiety, medications used for these disorders, and impaired sleep quality or quantity chiefly to DED symptoms. Obesity and face mask use have been linked to meibomian gland abnormalities. Studies of migraine, chronic pain syndrome, and fibromyalgia have mainly examined associations with DED symptoms. A systematic review and meta-analysis found increased odds of variably defined DED across chronic pain conditions, with odds ratios ranging from 1.60 to 2.16; heterogeneity warrants further work on DED signs and evaporative versus aqueous-deficient subtypes. Tobacco use has been linked most closely to tear instability, cocaine to reduced corneal sensitivity, and alcohol to tear-film disturbances and DED symptoms.

document_sections.heading: 1.1. What is lifestyle? What are the challenges?
document_sections.content: Lifestyle concerns how a person lives; a challenge can be a demand, provocation, or threat. Lifestyle changes over recent decades have improved quality of life, health, and longevity, but some may also challenge the ocular surface and contribute to more frequent or severe DED and other ocular surface diseases. This report examines that possibility within the Tear Film & Ocular Surface Society (TFOS) workshop on the direct and indirect ocular effects of everyday life. It addresses behavioral and environmental aspects of contemporary mental, physical, and social life. The term lifestyle does not imply that people deliberately choose to harm their eyes.

document_sections.heading: 1.2. An introduction to ocular surface disease and DED
document_sections.content: For this workshop, the ocular surface comprises the cornea, limbus, conjunctiva, lids, lashes, lacrimal apparatus, tear film, associated glands, and their muscular, vascular, lymphatic, and neural support. Ocular surface disease includes diseases of these structures and related disturbances and responses. DED is common in clinical practice, and cited studies indicate increasing prevalence. It is a multifactorial loss of tear-film homeostasis accompanied by ocular symptoms, with tear instability, hyperosmolarity, inflammation, surface damage, and neurosensory abnormalities contributing. Its manifestations include discomfort or pain, such as dryness, burning, or aching, and visual complaints; possible signs include aqueous deficiency, tear instability, epithelial disruption, inflammation, and meibomian gland abnormalities. Manifestations may occur alone or alongside Sjogren¨ syndrome, graft-versus-host disease, rosacea, seborrheic dermatitis, fibromyalgia, migraine, or diabetes mellitus. Aqueous deficiency is more frequent with systemic immune disease, whereas migraine more often accompanies symptoms disproportionate to signs. Lid and conjunctival anatomical abnormalities may induce or amplify tear-film changes. Accordingly, associations with lifestyle must distinguish symptoms from abnormalities of lids, glands, tears, and the ocular surface. The report also considers conditions beyond DED, including allergic conjunctivitis and pterygium, although most evidence concerns DED.

document_sections.heading: 1.3.1. DED symptoms
document_sections.content: Questionnaires address different DED manifestations. The Ocular Surface Disease Index (OSDI, range 0–100; higher scores indicate worse ocular symptoms) covers pain, vision, triggers, and quality of life. The 5-item Dry Eye Questionnaire (DEQ-5, range 0–22; higher scores indicate worse ocular symptoms) addresses dryness, discomfort, and tearing. The Numerical Rating Scale rates pain alone on a Likert scale of 0–10. The Neuropathic Pain Symptom Inventory modified for Eye (range 0–100; higher scores indicate worse symptoms) assesses five neuropathic-pain dimensions. The Ocular Pain Assessment Survey (range 0–200) assesses ocular-pain intensity regardless of cause. The review includes studies of diverse DED symptoms but excludes work focused specifically on neuropathic ocular pain because that entity lies outside its scope.

document_sections.heading: 1.3.2. DED signs
document_sections.content: The TFOS DEWS II Diagnostic Methodology report describes testing for DED diagnosis, monitoring, and classification. TearLab measures tear osmolarity; InflammaDry can indicate raised tear matrix metalloproteinase-9. Slit-lamp examination permits assessment of tear breakup time, dye-detected corneal and conjunctival epithelial disruption, tear meniscus height, Schirmer test results, and anatomical abnormalities of lids, lashes, conjunctiva, and cornea. Examples include anterior blepharitis, meibomian gland atrophy, meibum quality changes, conjuctivochalasis, pterygium, papillary changes, and epithelial basement membrane dystrophy. Corneal sensation can be assessed qualitatively with a cotton tip or dental floss and rated 0 = none; 1 = reduced; 2 = normal; 3 = increased, or assessed using a Cochet-Bonnet or non-contact corneal esthesiometer. Persistence of ocular pain after topical anesthetic during an anesthetic challenge suggests a central or non-ocular pain source.

document_sections.heading: 1.3.3. Relationships between DED signs, corneal nerves, and DED symptoms
document_sections.content: Ocular dryness, burning, aching, or tenderness often does not correspond to measured tear production or stability. Symptoms can predominate over signs with migraine or fibromylagia, while signs can predominate with diabetes mellitus. Differences in corneal nerve status may help explain this mismatch because these nerves relay ocular-surface information and can generate pain. Reduced sensation often accompanies neurotrophic keratitis and corneal staining; heightened sensation often accompanies neuropathic features such as burning and pain evoked by wind or light. Nerve abnormalities may occur alone or with aqueous-deficient or evaporative DED. This review addresses lifestyle-related DED symptoms and signs, not neuropathic ocular pain itself.

document_sections.heading: 1.4. Overview of review
document_sections.content: The report examines literature on lifestyle challenges and DED or other ocular surface diseases across mental health—depression, anxiety, coping, stress, and sleep—physical factors—inactivity, obesity, eye rubbing, sexual issues, pregnancy, chronic pain, and physical interventions—and social factors, including tobacco, cannabis, and other recreational drugs. It emphasizes epidemiology while considering mechanistic studies where available. Its physical-factors section additionally contains a systematic review and meta-analysis of chronic primary pain disorders and DED.

document_sections.heading: 2. Methods
document_sections.content: The narrative review summarizes reported associations and mechanisms connecting lifestyle challenges with DED components and other ocular surface diseases. Authors searched MEDLINE and Google Scholar non-systematically, selected relevant literature, and prioritized stronger methods rather than exhaustive coverage. Eligible published English-language scientific articles included original studies, meta-analyses, and systematic reviews. Searches combined ocular-surface, tear, corneal, conjunctival, DED, and related disease terms with mental-health, sleep, obesity, inactivity, rubbing, mask use, pain, sexual, pregnancy, tobacco, substance-use, alcohol, and caffeine terms. Authors also considered the workshop Evidence Quality Subcommittee database of appraised systematic reviews classified as Level 1, preferentially referring to reliable, high-quality reviews where possible. A separate protocol-based systematic review on chronic pain conditions and DED was registered as CRD42021296994; its methods and findings appear in section 4.6.6.

document_sections.heading: 3.1.1. What is depression?
document_sections.content: Depression is a persistent mood disorder involving sadness and reduced interest. It can present with fatigue, insomnia, unexplained pain, gastrointestinal complaints, or headache. People presenting mainly with bodily complaints may consult non-psychiatric physicians, allowing depression to go unrecognized and treatment to be inappropriate.

document_sections.heading: 3.1.2. Clinical assessment tools
document_sections.content: Instruments used in research on depression and DED include Beck Depression Inventory, Patient Health Questionnaire-9, and Symptoms Check List 90 (SCL-90). Patient Health Questionnaire-9 is a self-administered nine-question instrument based on Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fourth Edition criteria; it supports diagnosis and monitoring of depressive severity and has been validated in primary care and other settings. Symptom Checklist-90 contains 90 items with five severity-response options on a 1–5 scale and evaluates somatization, obsessive-compulsive symptoms, interpersonal sensitivity, depression, anxiety, hostility, phobic anxiety, paranoid thinking, psychotic symptoms, and additional complaints.

document_sections.heading: 3.1.3.1. Depression and ocular surface symptoms
document_sections.content: A 2017 synthesis of 28 eye-disease studies reported pooled depression prevalence of 25% (1502/6589 individuals, 95% confidence interval (CI) 0.20–0.30), highest in variably diagnosed DED (29%, 95% CI 0.17–0.40; five studies), followed by glaucoma (25%, 95% CI 0.18–0.32), age-related macular degeneration (24%, 95% CI 0.18–0.30), and cataracts (23%, 95% CI 0.07–0.40). Its geographic breakdown was 10 studies in the United States (US), 8 in Asia, and 7 in Europe. A 2021 meta-analysis of 31 variably defined DED studies reported depression prevalence of 40% (95% CI 0.29–0.52), odds 1.81 times those of controls (95% CI: odds ratio (OR) 1.61–2.02), higher depression scores in DED, and associations between DED symptom scores and depressive severity in several studies. In a case-control analysis of 2,454,458 US veteran records, 462,641 people had an International Classification of Disease (ICD) edition 9 DED diagnosis and 1,991,817 did not. After age and sex adjustment, depression and post-traumatic disorder each had OR 1.92, 95% CI 1.91–1.94 for DED. Depression occurred in 22% overall and in 24% versus 18% of those with versus without DED. A North Carolina study of 460,611 records, including 7207 with DED and 30,100 with depression under ICD-9 codes, found OR 2.9, 95% CI 2.7–3.1. A Netherlands study of 79,866 participants found adjusted OR 1.52, 95% CI 1.42–1.62 for self-reported depression and DED after accounting for 48 comorbidities and demographics; MINI-interview depression yielded OR 1.5, 95% CI 1.4–1.6. Among people not taking antidepressants, the association persisted (OR 1.6, 95% CI 1.4-1.8), suggesting medication-independent association. In a Taiwanese psychiatric-disease database (n = 75,650), DED affected 4.84% (n = 3665); depression affected 32.3% versus 23.6% of those with versus without DED (OR 1.54, 95% CI 1.43–1.65, p < 0.001). Among 472 Shanghai patients treated for depression and/or anxiety, 81% reported at least one DED symptom and 60% had both a symptom and sign. Age- and sex-adjusted DED associations included longer psychiatric illness (DED versus no DED: 54 ± 59 versus 39 ± 39 months), longer antianxiety or antidepressant use (17 ± 25 versus 10 ± 18 months), and selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor use. In a Korean survey of 16,408 participants, reported DED diagnosis (OR 1.32; 95% CI 1.11–1.57) and DED symptoms (OR 1.5, 95% CI 1.30–1.73) were associated with interview-assessed depression. A Hungarian study found higher Shortened Beck Depression Inventory scores in symptomatic than asymptomatic participants; Ocular Surface Disease Index and depression scores correlated at r = 0.31 (p < 0.01). Among 96 Singaporean ophthalmology patients with low tear breakup time, Center for Epidemiologic Studies Depression Scale scores were significantly associated with blurred vision but not irritation. A Shanghai study instead identified burning most frequently among people with generalized anxiety disorder compared with other psychiatric disorders. Symptom patterns may therefore differ across psychiatric diagnoses.

document_sections.heading: 3.1.3.2. Depression and ocular surface signs
document_sections.content: Among 657 Korean adults aged ≥65 years, depressive symptoms were associated with DED symptoms but not signs. The symptom association was stronger with Schirmer>5 mm (OR 3.08; 95% CI 1.93–4.93; p < 0.001) than Schirmer<5 mm (OR 1.52; 95% CI 0.70–3.30; p = 0.29). In Beijing (n = 1957), depression scores correlated weakly but significantly with DED symptoms (r = 0.07; p = 0.01), not tear breakup time (p = 0.18), Schirmer results (p = 0.37), corneal staining (p = 0.30), or meibomian gland dysfunction (p = 0.93). In 648 Netherlands participants with DED, depression increased the likelihood of symptoms outweighing signs. A German study found a higher mean Beck Depression Inventory score in DED than controls (11.95 ± 8.46; p < 0.0001), without a correlation between depressive severity and Ocular Surface Disease Index, tear breakup time, Schirmer results, or epithelial staining. Conversely, a Turkish comparison of newly diagnosed depression (n = 40), anxiety (n = 35), and controls (n = 37) found respective Schirmer results of 7.24 ± 6.02, 6.58 ± 4.9, and 18.79 ± 4.9 mm wetting (p < 0.05); tear breakup times of 5.6 ± 3.5, 5.62 ± 3.1, and 13.37 ± 1.7 s (p < 0.05); and Oxford scale staining scores of 1.9 ± 0.7, 2.1 ± 0.6, and 0.7 ± 0.4 (p < 0.001). Anterior segment optical coherence tomography tear-meniscus measurements were also more abnormal in the depression and anxiety groups (p < 0.05). Another Turkish study comparing 36 people with new depression and 32 controls found more abnormal Schirmer, tear breakup time, and Oxford results with depression. In 312 New Zealand residents, better self-perceived health was significantly associated with lower odds of aqueous deficiency and meibomian gland dysfunction. Thus, symptom associations predominate, although some studies also report more abnormal signs with depression; group means often remained within normal limits.

document_sections.heading: 3.1.3.3. Depression and tear biomarkers
document_sections.content: A study comparing 32 antidepressant-treated people with depression and 34 controls found higher tear interleukin-6, interleukin-17, and tumor necrosis factor-α in depression (all p < 0.001); a larger multicenter study (n = 535) did not reproduce differences in inflammatory markers by depression status. Another study found higher tear matrix metalloproteinase 9 (MMP-9), a protease involved in extracellular-matrix breakdown and leukocyte migration, in depression (n = 10) than controls (n = 21). In 23 stressed participants aged 21–53 years, relaxation response training was followed by significantly increased tear brain-derived neurotrophic factor and a non-significant decrease in tear nerve growth factor relative to pretreatment; cortisol and these factors were measured longitudinally in saliva and tears.

document_sections.heading: 3.1.4. Mechanisms
document_sections.content: Animal models have not robustly tested the depression–DED connection. Established depression models include reserpine-induced catecholamine depletion, learned helplessness, chronic mild stress, and social defeat. Brain-derived neurotrophic factor knockdown mice secrete fewer tears than controls, suggesting a possible mechanistic connection with depression and DED-related symptoms that requires further research.

document_sections.heading: 3.1.5. Depression and anti-depression medication
document_sections.content: Whether depression, its medication, or both account for DED associations remains unresolved. Studies assembled in the 2007 TFOS Dry Eye Workshop report associated antidepressants with DED. Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors inhibit serotonin transport and raise extracellular 5-HT. In a comparison of 36 treated patients with depression or anxiety in remission and 36 controls, users had tear breakup time of 7.05 ± 4.86 versus 12.53 ± 4.75 s (p < 0.001), Oxford staining of 0.78 ± 0.76 versus 0.11 ± 0.32 (p < 0.001), and Ocular Surface Disease Index scores of 32.07 ± 19.08 versus 16.31 ± 14.28 (p < 0.001). Clinical significance of the signs was uncertain because both groups' values were normal. Among 54 new antidepressant users and 57 controls, mean Schirmer wetting was 10.4 ± 5.8 versus 12.3 ± 0.7 mm; both means were normal. Schirmer score<5 mm occurred in 35% of selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor users versus 18.8% of serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor users, suggesting potentially greater effects of the former on secretion. A study of 20 users and 20 placebo controls found higher tear serotonin, more inflammation, and more ocular-surface cell apoptosis in users; rats given paroxetine for 6 weeks showed increased tear serotonin and expression of tumor necrosis factor-α, interleukin-1b, interleukin-10, and apoptosis genes. Another human study found no DED association with antidepressant use. A Netherlands study (n = 79,606) found no adjusted DED-symptom association with major antidepressant classes after accounting for more than 50 comorbidities and demographic factors; among people with depression, selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor use was associated with lower DED risk (OR 0.87, 95% CI 0.77–0.98). Those authors suggested that improvement of depression might outweigh potential anticholinergic DED risks and emphasized adjustment for underlying disorders.

document_sections.heading: 3.1.6. Treatment implications
document_sections.content: There are no standard guidelines for jointly managing depression and DED. In a secondary analysis of a randomized trial, DED signs and symptoms improved over time in omega 3 and placebo groups, while depressive symptoms measured with the Mental Component Summary of the 36-Item Short Form Health Survey did not change. This limited study suggests DED improvement does not necessarily improve depression scores. Interviews with 47 Chinese hospital patients with DED identified hospital-, daily-life-, and social-related sources of anxiety and depression; those investigators called for psychological interventions addressing these sources.

document_sections.heading: 3.1.7. Future directions and gaps
document_sections.content: Studies across populations and methods generally link depression more strongly to DED symptoms than to signs. Mechanisms and guidance for combined treatment remain unclear. Further work should investigate mechanisms, antidepressant contributions and timing, relevant DED phenotypes, confounding by pain or sleep, and optimal treatments.

document_sections.heading: 3.2.1. What is anxiety and post-traumatic stress disorder?
document_sections.content: Anxiety involves tension and intrusive or worried thoughts, sometimes accompanied by tachycardia or hypertension. Chronic, disabling forms include generalized anxiety disorder, obsessive-compulsive disorder, panic disorder, post-traumatic stress disorder, social anxiety disorder, and specific phobias; as many as 33.7% of people may experience an anxiety-spectrum disorder during life. Post-traumatic stress disorder follows trauma and may involve persistent intrusive recollections; it has been linked to DED frequency and severity. Uncontrolled anxiety has been implicated in worsening or treatment-resistant systemic and ocular chronic pain. Underlying anxiety and coping ability are important considerations when examining DED.

document_sections.heading: 3.2.2. Clinical assessment tools
document_sections.content: Clinical evaluation uses symptom assessments and questionnaires. Symptom Checklist-90 assesses nine psychological dimensions on a 1–5 range, with higher values indicating greater severity. Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder Checklist: Military Version is a 17-item instrument with range 17–85, with higher values indicating worse post-traumatic symptoms; it has been used in veterans. These and other instruments assist diagnosis and monitoring during treatment.

document_sections.heading: 3.2.3. Anxiety, post-traumatic stress disorder and DED
document_sections.content: Studies relate anxiety-spectrum disorders to several DED manifestations, more consistently to symptoms than to signs.

document_sections.heading: 3.2.3.1. Anxiety and post-traumatic stress disorder and a DED diagnosis
document_sections.content: Among 16,862 South Florida veterans, 12% had DED (n = 2056). Post-traumatic stress disorder occurred in 19% versus 11% of those with versus without DED and was associated with DED (OR 1.97, 95% CI 1.75–2.23); corresponding major-depression figures were 17% versus 10% and OR 1.91, 95% CI 1.73–2.10. After multivariable adjustment, associations persisted for post-traumatic stress disorder (OR 1.40, 95% CI 1.22–1.60, p < 0.0001) and major depressive disorder (OR 1.31, 95% CI 1.14–1.50, p < 0.0001). In a larger US veteran analysis (n = 2,454,458), 18% had DED (n = 462,641). DED associations included post-traumatic stress disorder (OR 1.92, 95% CI 1.91–1.94), depression (OR 1.92, 95% CI 1.91–1.94), antidepressant use (OR 1.97, 95% CI 1.79–2.17), and anxiolytic use (OR 1.74, 95% CI 1.58–1.91); all remained significant in multivariable analysis, with anxiolytic use the strongest overall predictor. In a Netherlands study (n = 79,866), self-reported agoraphobia (OR 1.9, 95% CI 1.5–2.4), panic disorder (OR 1.4 (95% CI 1.3–1.6)), and MINI-interview generalized anxiety disorder (OR 1.6, 95% CI 1.4–1.8) were associated with Women’s Health Study questionnaire-defined DED. Among 3,265,894 veterans, those with traumatic brain injury (n = 124,820) more often had DED (37.2% vs. 29.1%, p < 0.0005), post-traumatic stress disorder (54.3% versus 22.5%, p < 0.0005), and depression (69.0% vs. 42.0%, p < 0.0005) than those without brain injury. Veteran findings suggest a possible pathophysiological connection, but other populations must be studied before generalizing.

document_sections.heading: 3.2.3.2. Anxiety and post-traumatic stress disorder and ocular surface symptoms
document_sections.content: In 136 South Florida veterans, mean 5-item Dry Eye Questionnaire score was 11 ± 5.2 and 87% scored ≥6. Questionnaire and Ocular Surface Disease Index scores correlated with Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder Checklist: Military Version scores (r = 0.45 and 0.58 respectively, p < 0.05) and Patient Health Questionnaire-9 scores (r = 0.42 and 0.55 respectively, p < 0.05). Adjusted associations between post-traumatic symptoms and DED severity were 5-item Dry Eye Questionnaire: B = 0.07, SE 0.02, p < 0.0005; and Ocular Surface Disease Index: B = 0.60 SE 0.10, p < 0.0005; nonocular pain intensity also contributed, whereas DED signs did not remain in the symptom model. Among 248 veterans, 5-item Dry Eye Questionnaire scores were 13.4 ± 1.1 with post-traumatic stress disorder (n = 22), 12.0 ± 0.8 with depression (n = 40), and 9.8 ± 0.4 without either (n = 186; respective comparisons p < 0.01 and p = 0.02). Post-traumatic stress disorder (OR 4.08, p = 0.04) and selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor use (OR 2.66, p = 0.05) were associated with symptom severity in adjusted models; signs did not differ significantly. In 326 veterans, a discordance score based on Ocular Surface Disease Index and six signs was described as ranging from 1 for prominent signs to 1 for prominent symptoms. Anxiety (Symptom Checklist-90, r = 0.41, p < 0.005), post-traumatic stress disorder (Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder Checklist: Military Version, r = 0.46, p < 0.0005), and depression (Patient Health Questionnaire-9, r = 0.41, p < 0.0005) correlated with symptoms outweighing signs. Adjusted predictors included post-traumatic stress disorder (B = 0.21, standard error (SE) 0.02, p = 0.05) and depression (B = 0.01, SE = 0.005, p = 0.03). Post-traumatic scores also predicted symptoms on 5-item Dry Eye Questionnaire (B = 0.28, SE = 0.19, p < 0.001) and Ocular Surface Disease Index (B = 0.24, SE 1.35, p = 0.02). A Netherlands study of 648 DED patients likewise linked depression with greater symptoms than signs. Among 233 other participants, 5-item Dry Eye Questionnaire scores correlated with burning (r = 0.37), wind sensitivity (r = 0.37), and light sensitivity (r = 0.34, p < 0.001), as well as anxiety (Symptom Checklist-90; r = 0.21, p = 0.001) and depression (Patient Health Questionnaire-9: r = 0.34, p < 0.001). Veterans with neuropathic ocular-pain features (n = 51) scored higher than symptomatic veterans without those features on post-traumatic stress disorder (53 ± 21 vs. 36 ± 17, p < 0.0005) and depression (13.5 ± 8.1 vs. 7.6 ± 7.2, p < 0.0005), linking burning and wind/light sensitivity particularly with post-traumatic symptoms. In 87 Chinese DED patients, poorer National Eye Institute Visual Function Questionnaire function accompanied higher Zung Self Rating Anxiety and Depression Scales scores. Near-vision correlations with anxiety and depression were r = 0.31 and r = 0.33, p < 0.05 for both; distance correlations were r = 0.24 and r = 0.27, p < 0.05 for both. In 15,864 Korean participants, men with diagnosed DED and symptoms reported more stress (28.7% vs. 24.0%, p = 0.03), depression (9.3% vs. 6.1%, p = 0.003), and suicidal ideation (12.0% vs. 9.0%, p = 0.04) than those without symptoms; corresponding female comparisons were 35.7% vs. 28.1%, 23.2% vs. 17.5%, and 22.0% vs. 16.6%, all p < 0.001. DED diagnosis (OR 1.24, 95% CI 1.05–1.48) and symptoms (OR 1.47, 95% CI 1.27–1.70) remained associated with suicidal ideation in regression models. Studies generally associate worse DED symptoms with worse anxiety, but more work on visual function and non-veteran populations is needed.

document_sections.heading: 3.2.3.3. Anxiety and post-traumatic stress disorder and ocular surface signs
document_sections.content: Sign-related findings are inconsistent. In 87 Chinese DED patients, anxiety scores did not correlate with right- or left-eye tear breakup time (r = 0.09, p = 0.38 and r = 0.01, p = 0.92), Schirmer results (r = 0.04, p = 0.72 and r = 0.08, p = 0.45), or staining (r = 0.03, p = 0.77 and r = 0.04, p = 0.70). By contrast, a Turkish comparison of newly diagnosed anxiety (n = 35) and controls (n = 37), using Beck Anxiety Inventory (range 0–64), reported lower Schirmer wetting (7.24 ± 6.02 versus 18.79 ± 4.9 mm, p < 0.001), shorter breakup time (5.62 ± 3.1 versus 13.37 ± 1.7 s, p < 0.001), and higher Oxford scale staining (1.9 ± 0.7 versus 0.7 ± 0.4, p < 0.001) with anxiety.

document_sections.heading: 3.2.4. Mechanisms
document_sections.content: Inflammation is a proposed shared pathway. Reported serum elevations in post-traumatic stress disorder and depression include CD4:CD8 ratios, C-reactive protein, intercellular adhesion molecule-1, tumor necrosis factor-α, interleukin-1, and interleukin-6. DED has similarly been associated with tear or conjunctival CD4 lymphocytes and pro-inflammatory cytokines. In 133 Korean DED patients, tear interleukin-1β, interleukin-16, transforming growth factor-α, fractalkine, macrophage inflammatory protein-1δ, and epithelial neutrophil-activating peptide-78 rose with DED grade. Similar findings were reported in newly diagnosed DED and Sjogren¨ syndrome-related DED. Whether tear inflammatory patterns differ by anxiety or post-traumatic stress disorder remains to be tested.

document_sections.heading: 3.2.5. Treatment implications
document_sections.content: No prospective study has assessed whether treating uncontrolled anxiety changes DED. In a study of 45 clinic patients with DED symptoms, an individualized regimen that could include lubricants, fish oil, lid scrubs, warm compresses, tetracycline derivatives, topical corticosteroids, topical cyclosporine, or punctal plugs was given to moderately or severely symptomatic patients for 3–6 months. Baseline University of North Carolina Dry Eye Management Scale score was 5.8 ± 1.8, with 78% scoring ≥5; Generalized Anxiety Disorder 7-item scale score was 5.6 ± 5.5. At mean 13.8 ± 4.9 weeks, scores improved to 4.6 ± 2.2 (p = 0.01) and 3.3 ± 4.6 (p = 0.05), respectively, suggesting linked improvement after DED treatment. A separate rheumatoid arthritis study reported less joint improvement after treatment among people with baseline depression or anxiety than those without, raising the possibility that baseline anxiety may affect DED treatment response. Further research is needed.

document_sections.heading: 3.3.1. What are coping and resiliency?
document_sections.content: Coping refers to cognitive and behavioral efforts to manage demands judged to strain personal resources. Resiliency broadly concerns resistance to disruption and restoration of usual mental function. Deficits in these capacities differ from anxiety disorders, although inadequate resilience or constructive coping after psychological disturbance has been reported to affect DED adversely.

document_sections.heading: 3.3.2. Clinical assessment tools
document_sections.content: Healthy or active coping supports functioning despite pain; passive or maladaptive coping allows pain to disrupt life and foster helplessness. Catastrophizing includes rumination, magnification, and helplessness. Coping Strategies Questionnaire evaluates 8 strategies on a 0–7 scale, with higher scores indicating more maladaptive coping. Pain Catastrophizing Scale evaluates rumination, magnification, and helplessness across 13 items, range 0–52; higher scores indicate greater catastrophizing. Interference Subscale of the West Haven-Yale Multidimensional Pain Inventory assesses activity interference with 9 items scored 0–6 each, with higher scores indicating more interference. Connor-Davidson Resilience Scale has 25 items scored 0–4 each, with higher scores indicating greater resilience.

document_sections.heading: 3.3.2.1. Coping, resiliency, and DED
document_sections.content: In 194 South Florida veterans with DED diagnosis or symptoms, Pain Catastrophizing Scale scores correlated with 5item Dry Eye Questionnaire (r = 0.41, p < 0.0005), Ocular Surface Disease Index (r = 0.49, p < 0.0005), ocular numeric pain rating (r = 0.48, p < 0.0005), and Neuropathic Pain Symptom Inventory-Eye (r = 0.48, p < 0.0005). Tear parameters did not correlate with catastrophizing. Corneal sensitivity measured by Belmonte ethesiometry correlated at r = 0.17, p = 0.02, indicating greater sensitivity with more catastrophizing; InflammaDry correlated at r = 0.16, p = 0.02, interpreted as less inflammation with more catastrophizing. Multivariable analysis linked catastrophizing with worse symptoms and pain, not signs. Studies of nonocular pain have reported similarly sized associations. In 74 women with primary Sjogren¨ syndrome and 74 controls, 14-item Resilience Scale levels were similar, with median 78.5 in the Sjogren¨ group. Resilience was inversely associated with anxiety (p = 0.038) and depression (p < 0.001), not significantly with disease activity; specific DED outcomes were not assessed.

document_sections.heading: 3.3.3. Mechanisms
document_sections.content: Proposed links between maladaptive coping, resilience, and DED symptoms largely derive from nonocular pain research: altered daily cortisol patterns, increased inflammatory cytokines, impaired central modulation of incoming pain, and atypical activity in brain regions involved in anticipating pain. Functional magnetic resonance imaging has suggested potentially shared brain dysfunction in DED and psychiatric symptoms. Studies directly comparing markers such as interleukin-6 across compartments in people with different coping or resilience patterns are lacking.

document_sections.heading: 3.3.4. Treatment implications
document_sections.content: Mood-focused adjunctive treatment might help some DED phenotypes, but its effect in DED has not been studied. In a British trial of 598 adults with low-back pain, cognitive behavior therapy (n = 399) produced greater 12-month Von Korff pain scale improvement than control (n = 199): mean decrease 13.8% versus 5.4%, p < 0.0001, on a 0–100% scale. Acupuncture, exercise, and massage have also been studied for other chronic pain conditions. Effects of coping- and resilience-focused strategies on DED require investigation.

document_sections.heading: 3.4.1. What is stress?
document_sections.content: Psychological stress arises when perceived environmental demands strain or exceed a person's capacity to adapt and threaten well-being. Social and cultural change or globalization can create such demands. Potential domains include occupational and socioeconomic stress and stress accompanying depression or anxiety.

document_sections.heading: 3.4.2. Clinical assessment tools
document_sections.content: The physiological consequences of stress differ among individuals, so evaluation may combine subjective psychological assessments with physiological or biochemical measures. Ocular studies predominantly use self-report. Examples include a 3-point burden scale (1 minimal, 2 moderate, 3 high), a 4-point Likert scale (1 low, 2 moderate, 3 severe, 4 very severe), and Perceived Stress Scale 4.

document_sections.heading: 3.4.3.1. Stress and ocular surface symptoms
document_sections.content: Level 3 population-based studies report positive stress–DED associations. Among 1125 visitors to a London exhibition (707 females; age 33 ± 21), DED symptoms were measured with 5-item Dry Eye Questionnaire and signs with OCULUS Keratograph. Multivariable analysis linked poorer perceived health and greater stress with higher odds of Keratograph-defined aqueous-deficient and evaporative DED. In 312 New Zealand residents (178 females, 134 males), better perceived health was associated with lower odds of DED (OR 0.61, 95% CI 0.43–0.86), aqueous deficiency (OR 0.54, 95% CI 0.34–0.85), and meibomian gland dysfunction (OR 0.63, 95% CI 0.45–0.88). Greater reported stress was associated with higher odds of DED (OR 1.98, 95% CI 1.29–3.04), aqueous deficiency (OR 2.28, 95% CI 1.14–4.49), and MGD (OR 1.87, 95% CI 1.20–2.89), adjusted for age, sex, ethnicity, and contact lenses. Among 232 Korean paramedical workers, symptom-defined DED frequency was 42.7% (99/232); female sex, prolonged computer use, and higher stress scores were associated with DED, while sex and visual-analog stress remained associated after adjustment. Among 208 medical students, higher Perceived Stress Scale 4 scores remained associated with DED (OR 1.17, 95% CI 1.03–1.33; p = 0.014). In 211 adults aged 16–35 years, Ocular Surface Disease Index severity correlated with dry-eye quality-of-life (r = 0.67, p < 0.001), anxiety (r = 0.45, p < 0.001), depression (r = 0.54, p < 0.001), and stress (r = 0.44, p < 0.001). In a Korean survey of 6655 women aged 19 years or older during 2010–2011, diagnosed DED was associated with severe stress (OR 2.5, 95% CI 1.6–4.0), depressive mood (OR 1.5, 95% CI 1.1–2.0), anxiety/depression (OR 1.5, 95% CI 1.1–2.0), and previous psychological counseling (OR 1.8; 95% CI 1.0–3.1); analyses of DED symptoms showed similar patterns. Cross-sectional designs cannot establish direction or causality. DED-related limitations might increase stress, while stress might worsen ocular homeostasis through immune, hormonal, or neurosensory pathways. Longitudinal tests of either direction are lacking.

document_sections.heading: 3.4.3.2. Stress and ocular surface signs
document_sections.content: Most studies have not linked stress to ocular-surface signs. In young healthy adults, meibomian gland expressibility correlated with the anxiety subscale of the short depression, anxiety and stress scale (r = 0.15, p = 0.026). No other significant sign associations with its anxiety, depression, or stress subscales were reported. DED symptoms therefore appear more closely related to stress than signs.

document_sections.heading: 3.4.3.3. Stress and tear biomarkers
document_sections.content: Human studies relating stress to tear biomarkers have not been reported; this remains a research opportunity.

document_sections.heading: 3.4.4.1. Stress models and ocular surface symptoms
document_sections.content: Psychological stress can produce depression-like behavior through inflammatory, oxidative, apoptotic, and anti-neurogenic processes. Chronic mild stress models use unpredictable mild exposures; learned-helplessness models use uncontrollable aversive stimuli. Stress increases inflammatory factors such as tumor necrosis factor-α, but the mechanism and causal status of its DED association remain unclear. Proposed explanations include altered pain perception or somatization, systemic cytokine production with possible ocular inflammation, and confounding by stress-associated depression.

document_sections.heading: 3.4.4.2. Stress models and ocular surface signs
document_sections.content: Enriched environments have been reported to relieve manifestations of Alzheimer’s disease, Parkinson’s disease, and cancer, potentially through brain-derived neurotrophic factor activity. This factor is also implicated in stress symptoms, and its gene polymorphism has been associated with human DED. In one model, stress lowered its expression while environmental enrichment increased it; knockdown mice had reduced baseline tear secretion and impaired stress tolerance. Brain-derived neurotrophic factor may therefore connect stress with tear production.

document_sections.heading: 3.4.5. Treatment implications
document_sections.content: Persistent stressors are clinically recognized as possible triggers of fibromyalgia. A comparable triggering role in DED is plausible but unproven. Studies assessing whether treating stress improves DED, or treating DED alters stress, are lacking.

document_sections.heading: 3.4.6. Future directions and gaps
document_sections.content: Cross-sectional studies associate stress and DED, but longitudinal and treatment studies are needed to clarify their relationship. Such work should account for other mental-health conditions and medications. Animal stress models could help examine mechanisms difficult to investigate in people.

document_sections.heading: 3.5.1. What is a sleep disorder?
document_sections.content: Sleep affects immune, metabolic, aging, psychiatric, and cardiovascular functioning. Insomnia encompasses difficulties initiating or maintaining sleep and has multiple phenotypes. Other sleep disorders include parasomnias, excessive daytime sleepiness, and circadian sleep–wake timing disturbances relevant to shift work or jet lag. Distinguishing these from sleep problems related to medical disease, such as sleep apnea, or psychological illness can be difficult. More than one tenth of Australian and Korean adults were reported to experience excessive daytime sleepiness. Sleep disorders are associated with poor health, accidents, dementia, and mortality; their frequency and that of mental-health disorders increased after the COVID-19 pandemic.

document_sections.heading: 3.5.2. Clinical assessments
document_sections.content: Sleep evaluation includes reported outcomes such as Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index, Insomnia Severity Index, and Epworth Sleepiness Scale, as well as objective measures including actigraphy, laboratory or home polysomnography, and Multiple Sleep Latency Test. Questionnaires are faster and cheaper and useful for screening, but objective recordings are necessary for a formal diagnosis. Berlin questionnaire can screen for sleep apnea; Insomnia Severity Index and Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index can quantify insomnia symptoms and monitor intervention response. Because instruments serve different purposes, no single universally preferred questionnaire has been established.

document_sections.heading: 3.5.3.1. Sleep disorders and ocular surface symptoms and signs
document_sections.content: A systematic review and meta-analysis of 19 articles found poorer sleep quality, less sleep time, and more disturbances in DED than controls, with possible increases in sleep-disorder prevalence, incidence, and severity. Another systematic review reported more sleep disturbances, night waking, and pre-existing obstructive sleep apnea in primary Sjogren¨ syndrome than controls. Associated organic problems, such as urinary incontinence, may disrupt sleep in Sjogren¨ syndrome; Sjogren¨ and non-Sjogren¨ DED populations should therefore be considered separately.

document_sections.heading: 3.5.3.1.1. Sjogren¨ syndrome
document_sections.content: Database and clinic studies have linked primary Sjogren¨ syndrome with sleep disorders, assessing sleepiness, time to sleep onset, efficiency, fatigue, questionnaires including Epworth Sleepiness Scale, Improved Health Assessment Questionnaire, Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index, 10-point Mini Sleep Questionnaire, and objective polysomnography. One study used a longitudinal 15-item Dutch questionnaire. These studies generally found more frequent and severe sleep problems than in controls, but did not assess DED symptoms or signs within the Sjogren¨ population.

document_sections.heading: 3.5.3.1.2.1. Sleep disorders and DED in major population-based surveys
document_sections.content: Large Asian and Netherlands surveys have mostly assessed DED symptoms rather than signs and frequently used Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index; the accompanying table summarizes population-based studies. In Singapore, 3303 participants aged 40 years or older came from Singapore Malay Eye Study-2 (n = 1,191, 2011–2013) and Singapore Indian Eye Study-2 (n = 2,112, 2013–2015). Excessive sleepiness affected 6.4%, high sleep-apnea risk 20.5%, insomnia 2.7%, and sleep <5 h 7.8%. Adjusted associations with DED symptoms were excessive sleepiness OR 1.77, 95% CI1.15-2.71; high apnea risk by Berlin questionnaire OR 1.55, 95% CI 1.17–2.07 and STOP-Bang Questionnaire OR 2.66, 95% CI 1.53–4.61; insomnia OR 3.68, 95% 2.17–6.26; and <5 h sleep versus 5–9 h OR 1.73, 95% 1.17–2.57. The China Hangzhou Study linked poorer subjective sleep quality, longer latency, shorter duration, lower efficiency, sleep disturbance, and daytime dysfunction with greater Ocular Surface Disease Index symptom severity after accounting for confounders. A Japanese study found difficulty initiating or maintaining sleep and waking tired associated with DED in both sexes (p < 0.001). Relative to 8 h/day, shorter sleep was associated with DED in both sexes, while ≥10 h/day was associated with increased DED frequency among men. Comparing greatest with least difficulty falling asleep, adjusted ORs were 2.23 (95% CI 1.99–2.49) in men and 1.91 (95% CI 1.76–2.07) in women; relationships were stronger for severe symptoms than for clinically diagnosed DED. In 4185 Koreans aged ≥65 years, ≥9 h/day sleep was associated with lower odds of persistent DED symptoms (adjusted OR 0.52, 95% CI 0.33 0.83). In the Netherlands cohort (71,761 participants), 8.9% had DED; adjusted odds of poor sleep quality with DED remained elevated after correcting for >50 comorbidities (OR 1.20, 95% CI 1.11–1.28). Associations covered both sexes, age groups from 20 to 30 years through 70+, and all Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index components. Poor sleep quality affected 44.9% of those with highly symptomatic DED. Across surveys, associations between abnormal sleep and DED symptoms remained after confounder adjustment.

document_sections.content: The table summarizes population-based, cross-sectional studies comparing sleep measures and DED. Hanyud, 2021 [140], studied adults aged 40–74 years in Japan (total n = 106,282; n = 25,864 with DED) and associated poorer sleep quality and shorter sleep with DED. Magno, 2021 [142], studied adults aged 19–94 years in the Netherlands (n = 71,761) and found significantly poorer PSQI-measured sleep quality among those with DED. document_sections.heading: 3.5.3.1.2.2. Sleep disorders and DED in clinic-based surveys and crosssectional studies
document_sections.content: Clinic-based surveys and cross-sectional studies generally corroborated population studies, but measured sleep subjectively. A Japanese study of 301 people with clinically diagnosed DED found mean Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index scores of 6.4 ± 3.2 in severe DED (n = 146) and 5.5 ± 3.3 in mild DED (n = 155); the difference was significant, but healthy controls were not assessed [143]. In a Chinese cross-sectional study across n = 94 hospitals, McMonnies Questionnaire-defined DED (n = 17,937, 57.6%) was associated with sleeping-tablet use (multivariate OR 1.21, 95% CI 1.09–1.34) and tranquilizer use (OR 1.60, 95% CI 1.40–1.82); other sleep outcomes were not evaluated [144]. US insurance-claims research involving military personnel and families found significantly more insomnia and sleep apnea in DED than non-DED groups [145]; Korean claims research also associated sleep disorders with a DED diagnosis [146]. In an online survey of 2000 Japanese participants, those reporting DED described longer sleep latency, less sleep, and poorer sleep efficacy [147]. Obstructive sleep apnea has been associated with DED, conjunctival hyperemia, and meibomian gland dropout [148,149]. Greater interference with daily activities, including sleep, has been associated with worse DED symptoms [150]. In US veterans, at least moderate insomnia (Insomnia Severity Index score≥15) affected 61% of a high-ocular-pain group, versus 41% of a low-ocular-pain group and 18% of controls (p < 0.0005 for all). After adjustment, greater DED symptom severity on the 5-item Dry Eye Questionnaire was associated with insomnia (OR 1.1; 95% CI 1.01–1.2) [151]. Hospital-based evidence therefore supports an association chiefly involving symptom-defined DED; longitudinal research is needed to establish whether change in either condition influences the other.

document_sections.heading: 3.5.3.2. Sleep disorders and keratoconus.
document_sections.content: A cited meta-analysis pooled four hospital-based case-control studies and one large population-based cohort study. Most assessed obstructive sleep apnea with the Berlin Questionnaire; obstructive sleep apnea was significantly associated with keratoconus (pooled OR 1.84, 95% CI, 1.16–2.91) [152].

document_sections.heading: 3.5.4. Mechanisms
document_sections.content: In the mouse 'stick over water' sleep-deprivation model, 10 days without sleep produced epithelial damage, lipid accumulation, altered microvilli, and reduced tear production [153]. A subsequent 14 days of rest reversed these findings [154]. Topical palmitoylethanolamide during deprivation maintained the corneal barrier and improved clinical DED signs [155]. This model demonstrates objective ocular-surface and tear-secretory changes resembling human DED signs, although human research has not established a strong association between sleep disorders and DED signs.
