The reversibility and molecular findings may inform future interventions.

document_sections.heading: 3.5.4.1. Shared physiological pathways.
document_sections.content: Proposed pathways between disturbed sleep and DED include hormonal changes: sleep deprivation may lower androgens [156,157], disrupt circadian rhythms [158], and raise norepinephrine and cortisol, potentially affecting tear secretion [159]. Androgens influence lacrimal and meibomian glands; lower levels have been linked to DED [160]. Lacrimal secretion follows a circadian rhythm [161]. Hormonal imbalances involving serotonin, norepinephrine, and dopamine, and changes in the hypothalamic-pituitary axis, may affect sleep, mood, and DED [162]. Autonomic dysfunction is another possibility: sleep deprivation reduces parasympathetic activity, and reduced innervation can rapidly diminish tear flow [163]. Reduced brain-derived neurotrophic factor after sleep deprivation may also connect the conditions [49,164]. In a clinic-based comparison of 64 DED cases and 51 controls, DED was defined by symptoms, a Schirmer test value of <10 mm/5 min, or positive corneal staining and/or Rose Bengal corneal and conjunctival staining of ≥1. The minor allele A of the brain-derived neurotrophic factor Val66Met (rs6265) variant occurred in 18% of cases versus 9% of controls (p = 0.05; OR 2.22) [119]. In an intervention involving 20 healthy males, 10 underwent experimental sleep deprivation. Signs were evaluated at 2 p.m., 10 p.m., 6 a. m., and 2 p.m. the next day; at 6 a.m. after deprivation, osmolarity was higher and tear breakup time and secretion were lower than in controls [165]. Insufficient sleep might also impair ocular-surface repair: closed-eye tears have immunosuppressive properties, and release of antiproteases during sleep has been hypothesized [166]. CD66b-positive neutrophils have been detected in DED tears, raising a possible role for sleep-related prevention of degranulation [167]. Sequencing of closed-eye tears found more Streptococcus, Pseudomonas, and Proteobacteria in DED than control samples [168]. Evidence is insufficient to establish whether sleep disorders change the microbiome and thereby contribute to DED.

document_sections.heading: 3.5.4.2. Molecular pathways.
document_sections.content: Animal-study signs and microscopic observations suggest that peroxisome proliferator-activated receptors, alongside brain-derived neurotrophic factor, might contribute to the sleep-disorder–DED relationship [153].

document_sections.heading: 3.5.5. Treatment implications
document_sections.content: No randomized controlled trials were reported for this field. A pilot study followed Seventy-one patients with clinically diagnosed DED after eye-drop treatment, assessing Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index, Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale, photophobia, and chronotype. Follow-up by interview or mail occurred 3–10 months later and included a sleep diary, actigram, and medical interviews. Newly diagnosed patients improved more in sleep than patients with established DED; improvement in Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (p < 0.05) was strongly correlated with improvement in Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale (p < 0.05) only among new patients, suggesting a possible early treatment opportunity. An open-label study of 15 patients with DED and neuropathic-pain symptoms found better subjectively reported sleep at one week after a topical transient receptor potential cation channel subfamily M (melastatin) member 8 (TRPM8) agonist; ocular pain and tear production also improved at one month, and the sleep finding was not adjusted for these changes [169]. A crossover ocular-gel study found better visual-analog-scale sleep quality with hyaluronic acid/trehalose-based formulations but lacked an untreated parallel control group [170]. No sleep intervention study evaluated corresponding improvement in DED measures. DED prevalence and incidence increased more than in the general population for up to 3 years after initiation of continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) and nasal masks; absence of a control arm prevents a conclusive interpretation [171]. Melatonin improves sleep onset, quality, quantity, and circadian synchronization, but has not been studied specifically for DED [172]. Psychological and sleep disorders may be difficult to disentangle in DED. In a DED clinic, the report favors addressing both rather than only one. Blue-light-shield eyewear, blue-light therapy lamps, relaxation, cognitive rehabilitation, and mindfulness have been suggested without trial testing and require more rigorous evaluation [173,174].

document_sections.heading: 3.5.6. Future direction and gaps
document_sections.content: DED symptoms, including ocular pain, have been linked to insomnia and sleep–wake-cycle disorders, although both conditions are heterogeneous. Future work should consider anxiety, depression, extraocular pain such as migraine, menopause, andropause, mental health, and aging as potential contributors. Few interventions have been studied. Randomized trials should assess both the effect of sleep interventions on DED and the effect of DED interventions on sleep, while monitoring pain and psychological symptoms. Basic research should investigate molecular processes in sleep-deprivation-related DED, potentially informing interventions involving peroxisome proliferator-activated receptors or brain-derived neurotrophic factor.

document_sections.heading: 4.1. Physical inactivity and obesity
document_sections.content: This section examines physical inactivity and obesity in relation to DED and other ocular-surface conditions.

document_sections.heading: 4.1.1. What is physical inactivity and obesity?
document_sections.content: Physical inactivity denotes not attaining recommended regular exercise. The American Heart Association recommends 30–60 min of aerobic exercise three to four times per week. Average body mass index has risen in many countries alongside obesity, hypertension, diabetes, and obstructive sleep apnea. For adults, a body mass index of 18.5 to 24.9 kg/m2 is considered healthy, 25.0 to 29.9 kg/m2 overweight, and 30 kg/m2 or higher obese [178,179].

document_sections.heading: 4.1.2. Associations between obesity, DED, and ocular surface diseases
document_sections.content: Findings on obesity and DED conflict. In a Dutch population-based cohort (n = 79,866; 59% women; 9.1% with DED), higher body mass index (adjusted OR 0.985, 95% CI 0.979–0.991) and waist circumference (adjusted OR 0.995, 95% CI 0.992–0.997) were associated with lower DED prevalence [31]. A Japanese questionnaire survey of 85,264 adults aged 40–74 years identified DED in 23.4% (n = 19,985; 6289 men, 13,696 women); the adjusted OR for DED per kg/m2 increase in body mass index was 0.98 (95% CI 0.97–0.99) in men and 0.97 (95% CI 0.97–0.98) in women [181]. Conversely, among 305 Australian optometry patients, body-fat percentage correlated with symptom scores on the short form Dry Eye Questionnaire (r = 0.34, p = 0.003) and Ocular Comfort Index (r = 0.32, p = 0.004); after accounting for age and contact-lens wear, the association was significant in females but not males [182]. In 40 males, those with elevated versus normal body mass index (median 31.8 versus 20.5 kg/m2) had shorter mean non-invasive tear breakup time (8.5 versus 14.7 s, p < 0.05) and more abnormal tear ferning (2.0 ± 1.1 versus 0.7 ± 0.6 kg/m2, p < 0.05); tear-meniscus height and phenol-red-thread results did not differ significantly [183]. Among 175 US children aged 4–17 years, mean meiboscore was 0.82 ± 0.94 (range 0–4), mean tortuosity score 0.53 ± 0.70 (range 0–2), 56% had gland atrophy, and 29% had tortuosity score 1. Mean body mass index was 20.5 ± 4.86 kg/m2; 39.4% (n = 69) exceeded the 85th percentile. Body mass index percentile predicted tortuosity (OR 1.01, 95% CI 1.00–1.02), but not meiboscore. Percentiles 41 to 60 versus 0 to 20 were associated with greater likelihood of tortuosity score greater> 0 (3.79 times; OR 3.80, 95% CI 1.17–12.24) [184]. Obstructive sleep apnea, which commonly coexists with obesity, is associated with DED, meibomian abnormalities, and floppy eyelids. Among 80 Egyptian hospital patients with moderate-to-severe sleep apnea, conjunctival hyperemia and DED were more likely than in controls (OR 3.7 and OR 4.4, respectively), and tear breakup time was reduced in 45% of affected patients [148]. In Turkey, 36 people with severe versus 24 with mild sleep apnea had significantly more foamy tears, gland plugging, duct distortion, and higher total meiboscore; a proposed contribution from interleukin-1, interleukin-6, interleukin-8, and tumor necrosis factor-α was not directly tested [149]. Floppy eyelid syndrome has been linked to obesity and possibly tarsal weakening; its prevalence in sleep apnea has been reported as high as 32% [185]. Easily displaced lids may sustain conjunctival exposure and nighttime trauma, potentially compounded by airflow from continuous positive airway pressure. In Medicare data, DED prevalence among continuous positive airway pressure or nasal-mask users was 6.2%, 10.0%, and 13.0% at 12, 24, and 36 months, respectively. Comorbidities could account for some of this association [171].

document_sections.heading: 4.2. Physical interventions
document_sections.content: This section considers devices used for obstructive sleep apnea and masks used against airborne infection in relation to ocular-surface health.

document_sections.heading: 4.2.1. What are physical interventions?
document_sections.content: Here, physical interventions mean devices intended to affect, alter, or prevent disease. The focus is continuous positive airway pressure for sleep apnea and protective face masks against airborne disease transmission.

document_sections.heading: 4.2.2. Continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP)
document_sections.content: Continuous positive airway pressure devices used for obstructive sleep apnea or chronic obstructive pulmonary disease have been reported to induce or worsen DED [186,187]. Escaping air can dry the ocular surface. Ocular manifestations have been reported in as high as 50–70% of users [185,187], including floppy eyelid syndrome, shorter tear breakup time, and higher Schirmer scores [188]. Among 350,420 users (age 53.1 ± 11.8 years; 63.3% male), DED prevalence over 36 months was 13.0%, versus 6.7% in the general US population. Prevalence was higher in female users (14.9%, 95% CI 14.7–15.2) than male users (7.7%, 95% CI 7.6–7.9) [2,171]. In 72 users with sleep apnea, 67% met DED criteria of Ocular Surface Disease Index ≥13 plus at least one sign; floppy eyelid syndrome occurred in 26 patients (54%) diagnosed with DED [187]. Among 40 previously untreated patients with sleep apnea (age 52.48 ± 9.5 years; 80% male), ocular irritation rose from 42.5% before treatment to 57.5% afterward (p = 0.031) [188]. Mask designs and fit vary by patient; limiting leakage toward the eyes may reduce irritation. Providers should explain appropriate fit and nighttime artificial-tear or topical-emollient use to mitigate possible ocular effects.

document_sections.heading: 4.2.3. Mask-Associated Dry Eye disease
document_sections.content: Face-mask use has been linked to newly occurring or worsening DED symptoms, both with and without pre-existing DED [189,190]. The term MADE emerged during the early COVID-19 pandemic in response to clinicians’ anecdotal observations. In a survey of 3605 people, 68% reported mask-associated DED symptoms; 27% of these respondents reported worsening while masked [190]. Pre-existing DED may increase susceptibility. Wearing masks for ≥6 h per day, 5 days per week was associated with a greater increase in Ocular Surface Disease Index symptoms from before the pandemic than less frequent use [191]. Tear-film destabilization is suspected, but the precise mechanism remains unknown; suggested contributors include upward airflow with a poorly fitted mask and changes in temperature and humidity. In 66 DED patients and 62 controls, consistent mask use for 3 months shortened tear breakup time, increased surface staining, and was accompanied by corneal dendritic-cell density and human-leukocyte-associated antigen DR expression changes [192]. Effects were especially apparent with more than 6 h per day of use and occurred in both groups, but were greater in those with DED. Women and prolonged mask users may be particularly susceptible [193]. Mask wear has also been linked to more chalazia [194].

document_sections.heading: 4.3. Eye rubbing
document_sections.content: This section considers normal and pathological rubbing, associated ocular conditions, proposed mechanisms, and management.

document_sections.heading: 4.3.1. What is eye rubbing?
document_sections.content: Eye rubbing involves pressing the lids, often with fingertips or knuckles, and moving repeatedly to relieve itch or discomfort [195]. There is no standardized definition. Occasional rubbing associated with waking, sleep, fatigue, or transient irritation is generally benign; unusually frequent, forceful, or longstanding rubbing can be pathological [196]. Ocular-surface pruritus can stimulate sensory nociceptors and prompt rubbing. Its sensory processing overlaps ocular-pain pathways and involves behavioral, emotional, and motivational components, including the amygdala and GABAergic and dopaminergic neurons of the ventral tegmental area [197–203].

document_sections.heading: 4.3.2. Eye rubbing, DED, and keratoconus
document_sections.content: Prolonged or vigorous rubbing may alter ocular tissues and contribute to DED or keratoconus [195]. Reported associations also include corneal ectasia, conjunctivitis, glaucoma, iris and posterior-capsule complications, intraocular-lens dislocation, retinal detachment, and extrusion of implanted silicone oil [197]. Ocular allergy may be connected through rubbing or keratoconus, but evidence conflicts; one systematic review and meta-analysis of keratoconus and allergic eye disease was retracted in 2022 [204]. Among 61 patients with vernal keratoconjunctivitis and corneal ectasia, n = 53 had keratoconus and pathological rubbing was frequent [205]. DED with allergic conjunctivitis and asthma in children have also been linked to ocular allergy [206,207]. Contact lenses and chemical irritants can provoke rubbing by stimulating ocular-surface nociceptors; removal-relief rubbing associated with contact lenses may partly contribute to DED among long-term wearers [208,209,210,211,285]. Psychiatric conditions accompanied by chronic fatigue or stress have also been linked to rubbing [209]. Among 212 institutionalized patients, including Trisomy 21 (n = 30), neonatal asphyxia (n = 15), and pregnancy-related infection (n = 9), 7.5% (n = 16) had keratoconus and were more likely to rub their eyes than those without keratoconus (p = 0.008) [212]. A 2021 systematic review pooling six case-control studies associated rubbing with keratoconus (OR 6.46, 95% CI 4.12–10.1), but found heterogeneous studies with limited methodological quality and called for standardized measurement of rubbing frequency, force, and technique [213].

document_sections.heading: 4.3.3. Mechanisms
document_sections.content: The eye-rubbing literature is much more extensive for keratoconus than DED. Rubbing has been reported in 40–70% of keratoconus patients [214]. Force on the peripheral cornea may expose a weakened cone apex to distending intraocular pressure and promote ectasia [215]. Rubbing has also been associated with increases in tear matrix metalloproteinase-13, interleukin-6, and tumor necrosis factor-α, which might contribute to keratoconus [216–218]. Among 244 patients with keratoconus, 65.5% reported pathological rubbing [219]; in another study of 200 patients and 100 controls, 48% of patients reported substantial rubbing (p = 0.02 versus controls) [220]. Among 1027 healthy volunteers, keratoconus prevalence was 2.5% (n = 26; 95% CI 1.6–3.5); family history (OR 1.4, 95% CI 2.5–51.3) and rubbing (OR 6.3, 95% CI 1.6–24.3) were the significant multivariable associations [221]. Knuckle rubbing can produce globe indentation force >4.5kg/2.54 cm [198]. In 57 keratoconus patients, rubbing was reported with fingertips (n = 51%, 4.3 ± 3.1 N), knuckles (n = 44%, 9.6 ± 6.3 N), or fingernails (n = 6%, 2.6 ± 3.3 N) [222]. Sleep position is another implicated mechanical factor [223,224]. For DED, a proposed mechanism involves recurrent friction, stretching, and compression activating mechanoreceptors, causing pain and neuroinflammation, and potentially sustaining inflammation [225,226]. A rat study found more mast cells, degranulated mast cells, neutrophils, and macrophages in rubbed than unrubbed conjunctiva [227]. Human studies have not established how DED signs or symptoms vary with rubbing patterns. In 49 healthy people, tear breakup time fell after 2 min of rubbing (15.3–13.9 s, p = 0.0001), whereas the opposite unrubbed eye changed from 15.3–14.8 s (p = 0.096) [228].

document_sections.heading: 4.3.4. Treatment implications
document_sections.content: Rubbing alone generally does not require treatment unless an underlying disorder remains untreated. Clinicians should consider its potential short-term intraocular-pressure increases, corneal deformation and ectasia in susceptible people, and tear-film abnormalities, and address triggers. Particular attention is warranted for people with ocular allergy or inflammation, contact-lens wearers, and children with myopia [196,229]. Regular lid hygiene, ocular-surface care, and avoiding allergens and chemical irritants are described as helpful preventive strategies [196]. In persistent, potentially damaging cases, cognitive behavioral therapy may be considered. Screening for and treating less obvious causes such as dryness, corneal deformation, anterior blepharitis, or meibomian gland dysfunction should also be considered. Warm compresses and ocular massage could themselves produce rubbing-related deformation [198]. Pleasurable sensations from scratching can reinforce an itch–scratch cycle [203]. Where rubbing appears psychogenic and causes tissue injury without an underlying ocular cause, counseling may be insufficient and screening for psychiatric disease may be necessary [209]. New pathological rubbing merits assessment because it can signal underlying disease and lead to lasting DED or keratoconus. More work on neuroinflammatory mechanisms may improve future diagnosis and treatment.

document_sections.heading: 4.4. Sexual issues
document_sections.content: Sexual dysfunction and DED both occur frequently in the general population [231,232].

document_sections.heading: 4.4.1. What are sexual issues?
document_sections.content: Sexual issues encompass dysfunction affecting active or reproductive sexual life and may involve developmental, functional, endocrine, obstetric, sociocultural, or psychological factors [233]. Table 2 outlines categories and possible ocular-surface relationships.

document_sections.heading: 4.4.2. Association between sexual issues and dry eye disease
document_sections.content: Self-completed surveys in North American, British, and Asian populations found one or more sexual issues in 37–43% of adult women and 31–33% of adult men [242–245]. Sex-hormone-related connections between sexual issues and DED have long been studied at cellular and molecular levels, but the 2017 TFOS DEWS II report noted limited high-level evidence and a need to clarify these relationships [160]. Both conditions are common and increase with age; ocular-surface diseases often differ by sex, and both sexual issues and DED accompany impaired health and chronic disease. A survey in England identified vaginal dryness as the most common sexual issue among women [243]. Sex hormones might contribute to both conditions [160]. Unlike people with DED symptoms, only a small proportion with sexual dysfunction seek professional care [2,242,243,246].

document_sections.heading: Table 2 Sexual issues commonly investigated in the medical literature and possible relationships with dry eye and ocular surface diseases.
document_sections.content: The table groups gynecological, andrological, female and male sexual-function, fertility, gender-dysphoria, hormonal, and environmental issues. It distinguishes observed associations involving Sjogren¨ syndrome and graft-versus-host disease from relationships that have not been investigated and proposed explanations involving sex hormones or neuropathy. It also notes clinical literature on hormonal imbalance and DED and limited evidence concerning anabolic hormones and endocrine-disruptor exposure.

document_sections.heading: 4.4.2.1. Polycystic ovary syndrome.
document_sections.content: Small Turkish and Italian observational studies reported more DED symptoms, shorter tear breakup time, meibomian gland dysfunction, and epithelial abnormalities in polycystic ovary syndrome than in controls [249–253]. In an Italian study of 62 women with ultrasonographically identified polycystic ovaries, 16 had clinical and biochemical hyperandrogenism; 15/16 of those with polycystic ovary syndrome had DED symptoms and signs. Compared with isolated polycystic ovaries and controls, this group more often reported dryness and itching and had shorter tear breakup time and a higher percentage of goblet cells [246,251]. Elevated luteinizing hormone, reduced insulin sensitivity, risk of Type 2 diabetes, and an enhanced response to luteinizing hormone-releasing hormone may influence the ocular surface [160,254–256]. Further studies should account for variability in clinical and hormonal manifestations.

document_sections.heading: 4.4.2.2. Complete androgen insensitivity syndrome.
document_sections.content: Androgen-receptor gene mutations cause a female phenotype in 46, XY individuals with complete androgen insensitivity syndrome. Studies have linked the condition to DED [257,258]. In a comparison of 9 affected individuals with 10 age-matched women, DED symptoms occurred in 78% versus 14%, alongside more frequent tear-meniscus and meibomian abnormalities in the affected group [258]. Impaired androgen-receptor function is considered a likely contributor, given analogous findings with anti-androgen treatment [259]. Estrogen supplementation might further worsen DED, as estrogen administration has been identified as a DED risk factor [231,257,258].

document_sections.heading: 4.4.2.3. Graft-versus-host disease and Stevens-Johnson syndrome.
document_sections.content: Sexual issues have been discussed in DED-associated disorders such as Sjogren¨ syndrome, graft-versus-host disease, and Stevens-Johnson syndrome, rather than in DED generally [260–263]. Stevens-Johnson syndrome can follow a drug adverse effect or infection and cause inflammatory separation of skin and mucosa followed by scarring. It causes DED, ocular-surface injury, and genital scarring [263]. An association between its ocular and sexual complications has not been investigated; their coexistence is considered likely because of mucocutaneous fibrosis.

document_sections.heading: 4.4.2.4. Sjogren¨ syndrome.
document_sections.content: Sjogren¨ syndrome is an immune disorder associated with aqueous-deficient DED and impaired sexual activity. An Italian comparison of 24 affected women with 24 controls found lower sexual satisfaction before and after menopause, with significant differences in dyspareunia, lubrication, desire, and arousal; older age and anxiety contributed, whereas measured gynecological anatomical and cellular changes did not [261]. A Turkish study of 68 women with primary Sjogren¨ syndrome and 135 controls supported effects of age, menopause, and anxiety and found more genital atrophy. Clinically confirmed vaginal dryness and atrophy correlated inversely with Female Sexual Function Index scores [264]. Among 199 affected women in the Netherlands, vaginal dryness scores correlated with oral and ocular dryness on a 0–10 scale, inversely with unstimulated salivary flow, and positively with peripheral neuropathy on the Sjogren¨ syndrome disease damage index [234]. Low androgen levels are a proposed link among Sjogren¨ syndrome, sexual activity, and DED; in women, they might also accompany lower sexual desire [265,266].

document_sections.heading: 4.4.2.5. Hematopoietic stem cell transplantation.
document_sections.content: Hematopoietic stem cell transplantation can be followed by hemorrhagic gynecological episodes and premature ovarian failure. Associated graft-versus-host-disease can cause skin and mucosal dryness, including ocular dryness, and introital stenosis; possible causes include total-body irradiation, chemotherapy, and genital graft-versus-host-disease [105,264,267]. A Seattle comparison involving 161 transplant recipients found differences between women and men in the decline and recovery of sexual activity. After 5 years, dysfunction was reported by 80% of female and 46% of male recipients, versus 21% of controls [268]. A review of articles published from 1982 to 2014 reported that genital graft-versus-host-disease can produce sclerosis and markedly impair sexual function. It recommended routine gynecological consultations even for asymptomatic female transplant recipients, allowing earlier diagnosis and preventive treatment when needed [105]. Further clinical study is required to clarify how frequent ocular graft-versus-host-disease and DED relate to these outcomes.

document_sections.heading: 4.4.3. Relevance of sexual issues to dry eye disease
document_sections.content: Sexual issues in disorders associated with DED are frequent and affect quality of life. Published guidance advises attention to prevention and treatment of gynecological, obstetric, and sexual problems in Sjogren¨ syndrome, Stevens-Johnson syndrome, and graft-versus-host-disease [263,269,270]. Mucosal dryness can affect sexual activity, fertility, and obstetric outcomes. Potential DED-related sexual problems may extend beyond gynecological consequences of hormonal imbalance. Polycystic ovary syndrome, endometriosis, menopause, and persistent genital infections, including herpes simplex virus, may affect both genital tissues and the ocular surface through systemic or inflammatory pathways [160,271,272]. Mechanisms connecting female and male sexual dysfunction with DED require deeper investigation; Table 3 presents conditions in which the relationships remain poorly understood.

document_sections.heading: 4.4.4. Future directions and gaps
document_sections.content: Research should clarify epidemiological, functional, neural, immune, and psychosocial relationships among sexual issues, DED, and other ocular-surface diseases. The intended benefits are better understanding of shared mechanisms, improved diagnostic tools, and possible preventive and therapeutic strategies.

document_sections.heading: 4.5. Pregnancy
document_sections.content: This section examines pregnancy-related ocular-surface findings, possible contributors, and treatment evidence.

document_sections.heading: 4.5.1. What is pregnancy?
document_sections.content: Pregnancy extends from fertilization until birth; in humans it lasts about 288 days and comprises 3 trimesters: first, second, and third.

document_sections.heading: 4.5.2. Pregnancy and the ocular surface
document_sections.content: The association of pregnancy with DED remains debated. In a Nigerian longitudinal study of 134 pregnant women, DED symptoms and signs worsened in the third trimester and recovered 6 weeks after delivery. With thresholds of >10 mm on the Schirmer test, >10 s for tear breakup time, and >13 on the Ocular Surface Disease Index, DED frequency was as high as 78% [278]. In a Ghanaian cross-sectional study of n = 201 pregnant women, prevalence was 41% using Ocular Surface Disease Index ≥13 with tear breakup time <10 s or Oxford staining ≥3; frequency increased with gestational age [273]. Using a Schirmer threshold of 5 mm, prolactin, testosterone, and parity did not influence tear production [278]. A comparison of 46 pregnant women with gestational diabetes mellitus and 36 controls found similar tear flow, breakup time, osmolarity, and Ocular Surface Disease Index scores; the authors concluded that diabetes mellitus did not adversely affect the tear film or surface during pregnancy [279]. Although hormonal changes and maternal–fetal microchimerism have been proposed as possible links to autoimmunity and DED, number of pregnancies and microchimerism were not associated with DED or Sjogren¨ syndrome [264,273,280]. In 117 women undergoing assisted reproduction, 32 of whom gave birth, the number with Schirmer results <10 mm in at least one eye increased significantly in the third trimester (p = 0.02) and three months post-partum (p = 0.04); at other phases, tear production was comparable with baseline (p > 0.05) [281]. Comparative studies are needed to determine whether assisted-reproduction pregnancies differ from naturally occurring pregnancies. Lifestyle, weight changes, comorbidities, and environmental exposures may affect DED during pregnancy [279,282–284]. A Chinese study of 200 pregnant women associated gestational diabetes with higher blood phthalate levels; research is needed on whether environmental factors raise pregnancy-associated DED risk [286]. In a safety study of 4808 individuals, 936 received sodium hyaluronate 0.1%; congenital abnormality rates were 14.9% versus 12.3% among unexposed women. Findings were similar for diquafosol and 0.3% sodium hyaluronate [282]. Systemic DED treatments and therapies for associated inflammatory disease may raise pregnancy concerns. Existing studies define and classify DED inconsistently. Overall, clinical DED measures tend to worsen later in pregnancy, permanent damage has not been reported, and artificial tears have been shown safe for mother and baby [273,282,287].

document_sections.heading: Table 3 Medical conditions associated with sexual issues and dry eye or ocular surface diseases, where both conditions can interfere with lifestyle, and the relationships between the sexual issues and ocular surface problems are not well understood.
document_sections.content: The table lists genetic, gynecological and obstetric, psychological, and systemic conditions or therapies in which sexual and ocular-surface problems coexist. It includes Complete Androgen Insensitivity Syndrome, Mirage Syndrome, Polycystic Ovary Syndrome, pregnancy, refractory genital infection, depression, post-traumatic stress disorder, hematopoietic stem cell transplantation, Sjogren¨ syndrome, and Stevens-Johnson syndrome. Their sexual–ocular relationships are described as incompletely understood; for Stevens-Johnson syndrome, the table states that an association has not been reported.

document_sections.heading: 4.6. Chronic pain
document_sections.content: This section reviews observational evidence, potential mechanisms, and a systematic review and meta-analysis concerning chronic primary pain disorders and DED.

document_sections.heading: 4.6.1. What is chronic pain?
document_sections.content: The International Association for the Study of Pain defines pain as a sensory and emotional experience related to actual or potential tissue injury. Pain persisting or recurring for longer than three months despite treatment of its original cause, or because that cause cannot be successfully treated, is considered chronic and can itself become the main clinical problem [288–290]. Estimates suggest 20% of adults have chronic pain [291–295]. Chronic pain disorders are associated with aspects of DED, and chronic pain shares pathophysiological features with DED symptoms [296]. Observational findings are reviewed here; section 4.6.6 addresses a systematic review and meta-analysis [16]. In n = 3,265,894 US veterans, ICD-coded DED co-occurred with headache, migraine, temporomandibular joint dysfunction, central pain syndrome, fibromyalgia, osteoarthritis, and post-herpetic neuralgia [297]. Traumatic brain injury was associated with more DED under both tear-insufficiency and pain coding categories [59]. In a Dutch cross-sectional study of 425 DED patients, 17% reported at least one chronic pain syndrome. These syndromes accompanied worse Ocular Surface Disease Index symptoms, with 10 items significantly higher, but not worse DED signs; patients with chronic pain had significantly less corneal staining and higher Schirmer scores [298].

document_sections.heading: 4.6.2. Fibromyalgia and DED
document_sections.content: A Dutch cross-sectional study of 79,866 participants, with questionnaire-defined DED in 9.1%, associated fibromyalgia with DED [31]. A UK female-twin study of more than 3000 participants identified fibromyalgia among the strongest DED risk factors [299]. Taiwanese database research compared 25,777 people with fibromyalgia and 103,108 controls: DED incidence was 7.37/10,000 and 4.81/ 10,000, respectively. After adjustment, the odds of DED were 1.39-fold higher in affected males and 1.45-fold higher in affected females; age younger than 50 and psychiatric comorbidity also influenced the association [300]. A case-control study of 34 affected people and 42 controls found higher Ocular Surface Disease Index scores and shorter tear breakup time with fibromyalgia [301]. Overall, evidence suggests a closer link to symptoms than signs; larger case-control studies should assess whether measures such as Schirmer scores are reduced. Increased corneal sensitivity may contribute even without DED signs. In 36 people with fibromyalgia, central corneal sensitivity correlated with Ocular Surface Disease Index score (r = 0.44, p = 0.007) [302].

document_sections.heading: 4.6.3. Migraine and DED
document_sections.content: Population studies have reported significant migraine–DED associations, more consistently for symptoms than signs [31,176,299,303]. Reliance on self-report or disease codes to identify migraine limits earlier work. In a Turkish comparison of 50 migraine patients and 50 controls, Ocular Surface Disease Index scores were 45.21 versus 26.59 (p = 0.001); Schirmer scores were 14.39 versus 21.63 mm wetting (p = 0.001), and tear breakup times 9.54 versus 14.96 s (p = 0.001), although group means for signs were near normal limits [286]. In people receiving botulinum toxin for chronic migraine, photosensitivity and baseline DED symptoms improved independently of baseline tear volume: among those with initial 5-item Dry Eye Questionnaire score ≥12, scores fell from 15.4 to 13.8 (95% CI 3.02 to 0.19). The mechanism is uncertain; trigeminal-pathway modulation was proposed [307]. Different diagnostic approaches for both conditions create heterogeneity, so larger studies are needed to strengthen the evidence.

document_sections.heading: 4.6.4. Chronic pain syndrome (CPS) and DED
document_sections.content: In a population study of 1635 female UK twins, higher general pain sensitivity and lower pain tolerance were associated with DED defined by prior clinician diagnosis, artificial-tear prescription, or symptoms; a subset completed Ocular Surface Disease Index assessments [308]. In a cross-sectional study of 181 people assessed for DED symptoms and ocular and extraocular pain, more severe neuropathic ocular-pain scores accompanied more severe chronic pain disorders. Central pain syndrome occurred in 20% with high ocular-pain scores versus 7% with limited ocular symptoms [72]. A study of 8,564 predominantly female twins suggested shared genetic contributions to clustering of chronic widespread pain, pelvic pain, irritable bowel syndrome, and DED [309]. Chronic pain also occurred in a case-control study of 108 people with primary Sjogren¨ syndrome: 65% of seropositive and 75% of seronegative cases had chronic pain [310].

document_sections.heading: 4.6.5. Mechanisms
document_sections.content: Neuropathic changes in the trigeminal somatosensory system are proposed as one possible explanation for links between chronic pain and DED.

document_sections.heading: 4.6.5.1. Peripheral sensitization.
document_sections.content: Corneal nerves are environmentally exposed and vulnerable to repeated injury. Extensive damage to nociceptors can change their physiology, produce maladaptive plasticity and hypersensitivity, and ultimately contribute to neuropathic pain [311]. Proposed changes include altered ion channels, increased excitability, recruitment of neighboring nociceptors, and effects of inflammatory mediators released after injury [311–314]. Ocular-surface cold thermoreceptors monitor corneal moisture; their maladaptive responses to chronic overstimulation in DED may partly account for symptoms [315].

document_sections.heading: 4.6.5.2. Central sensitization.
document_sections.content: Prolonged peripheral nerve injury and persistent inflammation may reorganize central neural pathways, allowing pain without an ongoing peripheral stimulus or after injury resolves. This could help explain coexistence of ocular and systemic chronic pain [311,316–321]. Selective corneal-nerve injury has been linked to inflammatory cytokine expression in the trigeminal ganglion; direct central nervous system injury, as in traumatic brain injury, can also initiate chronic pain [318,322,323]. Trigeminal central sensitization has been demonstrated in animal DED models [324]. Preclinical findings implicate substance P in ocular-surface pain and inflammation [314,325], while clinical findings associate C-reactive protein with greater cold-evoked pain sensitivity [326]. Vitamin D deficiency has been associated with altered corneal-nerve morphology, dendritic-cell recruitment, and pain in chronic DED [327]. The literature more strongly connects chronic pain with DED symptoms than signs. Heterogeneity in design, methods, and populations requires further work. Future studies are advised to measure multiple DED symptoms and signs, distinguish aqueous-deficient from evaporative DED, and standardize pain assessment in line with International Association for the Study of Pain suggestions.

document_sections.heading: 4.6.6. Association between chronic primary pain disorders and dry eye disease: a systematic review and meta-analysis
document_sections.content: This section presents the report’s systematic review and meta-analysis of associations between chronic primary pain disorders and DED.

document_sections.heading: 4.6.6.1. Introduction.
document_sections.content: The TFOS DEWS II DED definition recognizes pain and neurosensory abnormalities [3], but the relationship of systemic pain with DED remains uncertain. Prior studies associated DED with migraine, fibromyalgia, and irritable bowel syndrome [328–332], possibly through shared neuropathic pathways; greater pain sensitivity could also affect symptom reporting. The review aimed to systematically identify, assess, and combine clinical studies evaluating DED among people with chronic primary pain disorders.

document_sections.heading: 4.6.6.2. Methods.
document_sections.content: The systematic review followed PRISMA 2 reporting guidance [333], and its protocol was prospectively registered in PROSPERO as CRD42021296994.

document_sections.heading: 4.6.6.2.1. Study eligibility criteria
document_sections.content: Eligibility covered study design, adult primary-pain populations, DED ascertainment, and odds of DED as the outcome.

document_sections.heading: 4.6.6.2.1.1. Study design
document_sections.content: Eligible publications were systematic reviews and retrospective or prospective observational case-control, cohort, cross-sectional, or epidemiological studies in English. Conference abstracts, case reports, case series, preclinical studies, and nonsystematic reviews were excluded.

document_sections.heading: 4.6.6.2.1.2. Participants
document_sections.content: Eligible studies compared DED in adults aged 18 years and over with a primary pain disorder against an internal control population. Primary pain meant pain in one or more anatomical regions persisting or recurring for longer than 3 months without a better alternative diagnosis [334]. Pain status could be determined objectively, by a clinician, from International Classification of Diseases records, or by self-report. Conditions considered under the International Association for the Study of Pain classification for International Classification of Diseases-11 included chronic widespread, complex regional, primary headache or orofacial, primary visceral, and primary musculoskeletal pain. Secondary pain, such as diabetic neuropathy or post-surgical or post-traumatic pain, was excluded.

document_sections.heading: 4.6.6.2.1.3. DED diagnosis
document_sections.content: Studies could establish DED through symptoms, signs, self-reported diagnosis, or International Classification of Diseases codes in clinical records.

document_sections.heading: 4.6.6.2.1.4. Outcome measures
document_sections.content: The review outcome was the odds of DED, stated as an OR with 95% CIs.

document_sections.heading: 4.6.6.2.2. Search methods for identification of studies.
document_sections.content: Ovid Medline and Ovid Embase were searched from inception through 9 December 2021 without search-stage date or language limits. References of included articles were also examined; Appendix A contains the search strategy.

document_sections.heading: 4.6.6.2.3. Study screening.
document_sections.content: Two of three authors independently screened search records in Covidence, first by title and abstract and then by full text. Reasons for full-text exclusion were recorded, and eligibility disagreements were resolved by discussion and consensus.

document_sections.heading: 4.6.6.2.4. Data extraction.
document_sections.content: Two reviewers independently extracted bibliographic and setting details, design and recruitment, group size and participant characteristics, pain diagnoses and assessment, DED criteria and assessment, funding, conflicts, numbers with DED, and ORs. Disagreements were settled by consensus. Adjusted ORs were preferred when available to limit confounding [335]. Investigators of the included studies were not contacted.

document_sections.heading: 4.6.6.2.5. Risk of bias assessment.
document_sections.content: Two reviewers independently and blindly assessed risk of bias, resolving differences by consensus. They used AMSTAR-2 for systematic reviews and the Newcastle-Ottawa scale for observational studies. AMSTAR-2 has 16 domains, seven considered critical to review validity [336]. Newcastle-Ottawa assesses selection, comparability, and outcomes, with a maximum of nine stars [337].

document_sections.heading: 4.6.6.2.6. Data synthesis.
document_sections.content: Statistical analyses used R Project for Statistical Computing [338].

document_sections.heading: 4.6.6.2.6.1. Meta-analysis
document_sections.content: Results for the same primary pain disorder were pooled when at least three studies supplied outcomes. Analyses used the participant as the unit and estimated ORs with 95% CIs. Precalculated binary effects were pooled after log transformation of ORs and intervals using a random-effects inverse-variance model. If an OR was unavailable, group counts of DED cases were converted to an OR.

document_sections.heading: 4.6.6.2.6.2. Assessment of heterogeneity
document_sections.content: The reviewers compared participant characteristics and DED definitions to assess clinical and methodological heterogeneity, pooling only the same pain condition. Forest plots, I2, and τ2 were used to examine statistical heterogeneity, including effect direction and magnitude. I2 of 60% or more was treated as compatible with moderate statistical heterogeneity [335]. Considerably heterogeneous findings could still be pooled if individual effects pointed in the same direction. A prediction interval was planned when more than ten studies entered a meta-analysis; otherwise, findings were described.

document_sections.heading: 4.6.6.2.6.3. Sensitivity analysis
document_sections.content: Where heterogeneity exceeded >60% and at least three studies remained, sensitivity analyses excluded studies defining DED solely through self-report or retrospective records or coding, retaining clinical symptom or sign assessments.

document_sections.heading: 4.6.6.2.6.4. Subgroup analysis
document_sections.content: Subgroup analyses by aqueous-deficient versus evaporative DED had been planned, but too few studies reported subtypes.

document_sections.heading: 4.6.6.2.6.5. Reporting bias
document_sections.content: For meta-analyses with at least 10 studies, funnel plots were planned to investigate potential publication bias through visual assessment of asymmetry.

document_sections.heading: 4.6.6.2.7. Certainty of the evidence.
document_sections.content: Certainty for each synthesis was assessed with the Grading of Recommendations, Assessment, Development and Evaluation (GRADE) approach [339]. Reasons for ratings are presented in Supplementary Table S1.

document_sections.heading: 4.6.6.3. Results
document_sections.content: The results section reports study identification and characteristics, followed by assessments and pooled findings.

document_sections.heading: 4.6.6.3.1. Description of studies.
document_sections.content: Electronic searches found 1570 records. Following duplicate removal, 1417 studies were screened and 23 included: one systematic review and 22 observational studies, described as 16 prospective cross-sectional studies, two retrospective case-control studies, and three retrospective chart reviews. Table 4 describes included-study characteristics; Supplementary Table S2 gives full-text exclusion reasons and Table S3 summarizes funding sources.

document_sections.heading: 4.6.6.3.1.1. Populations
document_sections.content: The included studies enrolled between 38 and 3,265,894 people. Most included men and women; among these studies, the proportion of women ranged from 24% to 94%. Table 4 describes the included studies. One population-based study and two fibromyalgia studies enrolled only women. Four studies examined several pain conditions, whereas 19 examined a single primary pain condition: 11 addressed migraine, five fibromyalgia, and three irritable bowel syndrome. Of the 23 included studies, 11 described other comorbidities and six reported concomitant medication use.

document_sections.heading: Table 4 Characteristics of studies included in the systematic review exploring the relationship between DED and pain conditions outside the eye.
document_sections.content: The table describes each included study’s design, country, participants, pain-condition diagnostic criteria, DED diagnostic criteria, and DED outcomes. Its study groups cover multiple pain conditions, migraine, fibromyalgia, and irritable bowel syndrome.

document_sections.heading: 4.6.6.3.1.2. DED assessments
document_sections.content: Among the 22 observational studies, 11 assessed both DED symptoms and signs, five assessed symptoms alone, one assessed signs alone, and five used International Classification of Diseases codes from records or databases. Eight studies assessing symptoms used the Ocular Surface Disease Index, and two used the 5-item Dry Eye Questionnaire. Only one study applied the 2017 TFOS DEWS II diagnostic criteria, which incorporate symptoms and signs.

document_sections.heading: 4.6.6.3.2. Risk of bias
document_sections.content: The systematic review by Chen et al. had high risk of bias in eight of the 16 AMSTAR domains and was rated critically low in quality; its synthesis may therefore be inaccurate. Under the Newcastle-Ottawa tool, seven of the 22 observational studies received seven out of nine stars, while the lowest score was four out of nine stars. Participant selection posed the greatest concern: 16 studies received fewer than two stars out of four in that domain. Pain cases lacked independent validation in 16 studies, and 11 did not describe their participant recruitment strategy.

document_sections.heading: 4.6.6.3.3.1. Migraine
document_sections.content: Fifteen articles addressed DED in migraine: one systematic review and 14 observational studies. Migraine was self-reported in n = 6, identified through International Classification of Diseases codes in n = 4, diagnosed by a clinician in n = 2, and assessed by an unclear method in n = 2. Pooling 11 studies gave 1.61 (95% CI 1.39–1.87) times higher odds of DED with migraine than without migraine. Heterogeneity was substantial (I2 = 88%); the prediction interval was 0.98 to 2.65, so a future study might find no association. GRADE certainty was very low. Three studies without a dichotomous DED outcome were excluded from that synthesis. Sarac et al. and Koktekir et al. reported worse Ocular Surface Disease Index scores, Schirmer test values, fluorescein tear breakup times, and corneal fluorescein or conjunctival lissamine green staining in migraine groups (total n = 79) than controls (total n = 88). Shetty et al. reported greater Lipiview lipid thickness with migraine but no tear breakup time difference between migraine (n = 30) and control (n = 30) groups. A separate review by Chen et al. pooled seven studies also included in this report and found greater DED morbidity with migraine (OR 1.55; 95% CI 1.32–1.82; p < 0.001); methodological concerns may compromise that finding.

document_sections.heading: 4.6.6.3.3.2. Fibromyalgia
document_sections.content: Nine studies compared DED in people with and without fibromyalgia. Fibromyalgia was self-reported in n = 3, diagnosed using American College of Rheumatology 1990 criteria in n = 3, identified through International Classification of Diseases codes in n = 2, and assessed by an unclear method in n = 1. Pooling six studies yielded 1.91 (95% CI 1.63–2.24) times higher odds of DED with fibromyalgia. Heterogeneity was substantial (I2 = 84%), and GRADE certainty was very low. Gallar et al. could not contribute an OR because none of the 18 controls reported DED symptoms; 18 of 20 participants with fibromyalgia did report symptoms. Two further studies lacked a dichotomous DED outcome. Erkan Turan et al. found worse Ocular Surface Disease Index scores, tear breakup time, and lissamine green grading in the fibromyalgia group (n = 34) than controls (n = 42), without a Schirmer test difference. Türkyilmaz et al. reported worse Ocular Surface Disease Index, tear breakup time, Schirmer scores, and tear osmolarity in the fibromyalgia group (n = 53) than controls (n = 53).

document_sections.heading: 4.6.6.3.3.3. Irritable bowel syndrome
document_sections.content: Six studies compared DED in participants with and without irritable bowel syndrome. Diagnosis relied on self-report in n = 1, International Classification of Diseases database codes in n = 1, and ROME III or IV criteria in n = 4. A five-study meta-analysis found 2.16 (95% CI 1.65–2.82) times higher odds of DED in people with irritable bowel syndrome. Heterogeneity was substantial (I2 = 85%), although individual estimates pointed in the same direction; GRADE certainty was low. Uçar et al. did not report a dichotomous DED assessment and was excluded from the meta-analysis. That study found higher Ocular Surface Disease Index scores (p = 0.008) and lower tear breakup time in participants with irritable bowel syndrome (n = 29) than controls (n = 37).

document_sections.heading: 4.6.6.3.3.4. Back pain
document_sections.content: Three studies provided DED data for people with back pain. Back pain was identified by International Classification of Diseases database coding in n = 1 and self-reported in n = 2. Pooled odds of DED were 1.60 (95% CI 1.39–1.83) times higher with back pain than without it. Heterogeneity was substantial (I2 = 63%), but study effects pointed in the same direction. GRADE certainty was very low.

document_sections.heading: 4.6.6.3.3.5. Other pain conditions
document_sections.content: Three studies also examined other primary pain conditions. Chang et al. reported odds of symptoms meeting a 5-item Dry Eye Questionnaire score >5, relative to people without the respective pain condition, of 4.63 (95% CI 2.10–10.22) for muscle pain, 2.14 (1.16–3.95) for headaches, and 1.06 (0.33–3.44) for tendonitis. In US veterans’ records, Lee et al. reported odds of International Classification of Diseases-9-coded tear film dysfunction of 1.61 (1.58–1.63) for tension headache, 1.82 (1.81–1.83) for temporomandibular joint dysfunction, 1.75 (1.74–1.76) for abdominal pain, 1.57 (1.54–1.60) for pelvic pain, 1.95 (1.77–2.15) for central pain syndrome, and 1.57 (1.56–1.58) for recorded chronic pain or chronic pain syndrome. The Twins UK study reported an association of 1.86 (1.41–2.46) between self-reported DED diagnosis and pelvic pain.

document_sections.heading: 4.6.6.3.4. Publication bias
document_sections.content: The funnel plot for DED and migraine contained relatively few small studies reporting weaker associations, suggesting possible publication bias.

document_sections.heading: 4.6.6.3.5. Sensitivity analysis
document_sections.content: Table 5 compares the main analyses with analyses excluding studies that identified DED solely through self-report or retrospective diagnostic coding rather than clinical assessment of symptoms or signs. For migraine, heterogeneity fell from 88% to 36%. For fibromyalgia, the sensitivity-analysis account reports a fall from 81% to 0%, whereas the preceding effects summary reports I2 = 84% for the main analysis. For irritable bowel syndrome, heterogeneity remained substantial (I2 = 79%). Too few back-pain studies were available for this sensitivity analysis. The changes for migraine and fibromyalgia suggest that differences in DED diagnosis may contribute to between-study variability.

document_sections.heading: Table 5 Sensitivity analysis excluding studies that did not evaluate dry eye disease (DED) using clinical assessments of symptoms or signs.
document_sections.content: The table presents each eligible pain condition’s main and restricted pooled effects, heterogeneity, number of included studies, and studies removed by the restriction. It reports migraine main and restricted estimates of 1.61 (1.39–1.87), I2 88%, 11 studies, and 1.42 (1.17–1.72), I2 36%, 5 studies; fibromyalgia estimates of 1.91 (1.63–2.24), I2 81%, 6 studies, and 2.21 (2.03–2.41), I2 0%, 3 studies; and irritable bowel syndrome estimates of 2.16 (1.65–2.82), I2 85%, 5 studies, and 2.89 (1.50–5.54), I2 79%, 3 studies. The document gives a different fibromyalgia main-analysis I2 in the preceding effects summary.

document_sections.heading: 4.6.6.4. Discussion
document_sections.content: The review included 23 studies and found positive pooled associations of DED with migraine, fibromyalgia, irritable bowel syndrome, and back pain. The discussion describes 18 studies as prospective cross-sectional and five as retrospective reviews of existing records; most enrolled both sexes, and sample sizes ranged from 38 to 3,265,894. Differences in designs and populations probably contributed to heterogeneity. GRADE certainty was very low for migraine, fibromyalgia, and back pain and low for irritable bowel syndrome, so true effects could differ substantially from pooled estimates. All four estimates were downgraded for bias; most studies scored five or six stars out of nine. No study exceeded seven out of nine on the Newcastle-Ottawa tool. Inadequate descriptions of case definitions and sampling create selection-bias concerns and restrict generalizability. Studies should specify how pain conditions and DED were diagnosed. Diagnostic variation may also explain heterogeneity: only nine studies used clinical criteria for pain diagnoses, while others used self-report, diagnostic codes, or unclear methods. Eleven assessed both DED signs and symptoms, but only three of the 15 studies classifying DED dichotomously incorporated both; one of these used the TFOS DEWS II criteria published in 2017. Because too few studies used composite DED criteria, the authors could not pool only studies using that approach. Symptom–sign discordance, particularly in chronic pain syndrome, further complicates comparisons.

document_sections.heading: 4.6.6.4.1. Implications for clinical practice and future research
document_sections.content: Observed associations link DED with migraine, fibromyalgia, irritable bowel syndrome, and back pain, but low or very low certainty and substantial heterogeneity prevent precise confidence in their strength. The authors nevertheless state that patients with these pain conditions should be carefully screened for DED. They call for consistent designs and diagnostic definitions, clear clinical pain criteria, and a core classification such as the International Association for the Study of Pain classification of chronic pain. Medication effects and whether pain severity affects DED likelihood or severity warrant study; only six of the 23 studies reported concomitant medications. Future DED assessments should use best-practice criteria covering symptoms and signs, such as TFOS DEWS II, and distinguish aqueous deficient from evaporative DED to reduce heterogeneity.

document_sections.heading: 5. Psychosocial factors
document_sections.content: This part examines tobacco, cannabis, other recreational drugs, alcohol, and caffeine in relation to DED and other ocular surface conditions.

document_sections.heading: 5.1. Tobacco use
document_sections.content: According to the cited World Health Organization report, tobacco use is declining worldwide. Among men aged 15 years and older, use was reported for half in 2000 and projected at 35.1% in 2025; among women of those ages, the corresponding figures were 16.7% and a projected 6.7%.

document_sections.heading: 5.1.1. What is tobacco use?
document_sections.content: Tobacco use encompasses smoked products, smokeless products, or both. Its prevalence is declining in developed countries but rising in low- and middle-income countries; more than 1.3 billion people aged 15 years or older use tobacco worldwide.

document_sections.heading: 5.1.1.1. Impact of tobacco use
document_sections.content: Tobacco imposes health and economic burdens, including diversion of household resources from essentials and healthcare and productivity costs. Because related disease can take years to become apparent, morbidity and mortality may rise even while prevalence falls. The cited estimate attributes over 8 million deaths annually to tobacco: 7 million to direct use and 1.2 million to second-hand exposure. The World Health Organization monitors six MPOWER measures addressing consumption surveillance, smoke protection, cessation help, warnings, advertising restrictions, and taxation. The report states that at least one such measure protects 5.3 billion people across 115 countries and that the number of countries with best-practice cessation policies has more than doubled.

document_sections.heading: 5.1.1.2. Ingredients in tobacco
document_sections.content: The American Lung Association identifies over 600 ingredients in cigarettes or their smoke, including nicotine, acetone, benzene, formaldehyde, cadmium, acetic acid, carbon monoxide, tar, and ammonia. In 2012, the Food and Drug Administration listed 93 potentially harmful constituents, classifying them by carcinogenic, respiratory, cardiovascular, reproductive or developmental, and addictive effects; established measurement methods exist for only 20 of the 93. Many countries lack cigarette-composition guidance. Cigarette constituents present substantial carcinogenic risk, including through passive exposure.

document_sections.heading: 5.1.2. Tobacco and ocular surface diseases
document_sections.content: The following subsections distinguish evidence on DED diagnosis, ocular surface signs, other ocular surface diseases, corneal characteristics, mechanisms, and clinical implications.

document_sections.heading: 5.1.2.1. Tobacco and DED
document_sections.content: Studies of active or passive smoking and DED report positive, negative, or absent associations. Differences in study purpose, ascertainment, smoking definitions, DED definitions, and statistical power may contribute. A 2016 meta-analysis of 10 studies—eight cross-sectional and two cohort studies, predominantly from Asia—found no significant age- and sex-adjusted overall association and had methodological limitations. Restriction to three general-population studies produced OR 1.50, 95% CI 1.08–2.09. Its authors suggested that population sampling, size, symptom-only DED definitions, self-reported smoking, and few smokers might affect results, leaving the relationship inconclusive. In an oral omega-3 DED trial, current daily smoking was unrelated to symptom or sign severity; only n = 26 of n = 535 participants were current smokers. Having ever smoked was associated with worse signs. This review describes studies with positive, absent, or possibly mild associations in chronic or heavy smokers. In a Netherlands cohort (n = 79,866), current smokers represented 12.6% of the DED group and 16.1% of the non-DED group (p < 0.001); compared with never smoking, current smoking had adjusted OR 0.87, 95% CI 0.80–0.94, whereas former smoking had adjusted OR 1.09, 95% CI 1.03–1.15. Overall, any relationship between smoking history and DED may be weak, and available higher-quality evidence remains inconclusive.

document_sections.heading: 5.1.2.1.1. Tobacco and ocular surface signs
document_sections.content: Studies comparing smokers with non-smokers or examining smoking subgroups often identify altered tear stability and epithelial measures. Among 88 Japanese office workers, smokers had lower tear production, goblet-cell density, and tear mucin 5AC concentration. In a Saudi eye-clinic sample of 250, all 44 smokers met symptom-and-sign DED criteria, with reduced tear breakup time most closely associated with smoking. A university study comparing 30 healthy male smokers with age-matched non-smokers found lower tear breakup time, more abnormal tear ferning, and higher McMonnies symptom scores in smokers. Among waterpipe smokers (n = 33) and non-smokers (n = 31) in Jordan, smokers had higher osmolarity and corneal fluorescein staining and shorter tear breakup time, but similar Ocular Surface Disease Index scores. Waterpipe smoke exposes users and nearby people to nicotine and cigarette-smoke toxicants; its passage through water does not establish reduced risk. In Malaysia, smokers (n = 27) versus non-smokers (n = 32) had shorter tear breakup time, more nasal and temporal corneal staining, fewer goblet cells, and higher McMonnies and Ocular Surface Disease Index scores. A Brazilian student survey enrolled 2158 participants; 54 underwent ocular examination and 5.6% of the full sample smoked. Higher Ocular Surface Disease Index scores were associated with smoking after adjustment, but examination results were not broken down by smoking status. Across these younger groups, signs generally appeared worse in smokers, whereas symptom differences varied. An Indian clinic comparison of 50 smokers and 50 non-smokers found lower tear breakup time and corneal sensitivity with smoking, while anesthetized Schirmer results were normal in both groups at ~20 mm wetting per 5 min; investigators proposed lipid peroxidation and nerve toxicity. A Turkish comparison of 50 heavy smokers and 50 non-smokers found higher symptom scores, shorter tear breakup time, and fewer goblet cells in smokers, without differences in corneal staining or Schirmer results. In another Japanese comparison, 25 healthy smokers versus 20 non-smokers aged 20–45 years had reduced tear breakup time, goblet-cell density, and tear spreading; symptoms were not present in all smokers (80%). A separate Turkish study found higher symptom scores and tear production but lower tear breakup time and lysozyme concentration in smokers (n = 44) versus non-smokers (n = 37), with comparable goblet-cell density and rose bengal staining. In a comparison of 21 vapers and 21 healthy non-smokers, vaping was associated with more DED symptoms, shorter tear breakup time, greater corneal staining, and lower tear meniscus height, but not lower Schirmer tear production. Tobacco initiation, including vaping, commonly occurs before age 18 years. Passive-smoke chamber studies in non-smokers found increased tear inflammatory cytokines and lipid-peroxidation products and reduced mucin function; exposed contact-lens wearers showed tear instability and epithelial injury. In a prospective study of 112 children with eye discomfort, 80 (71%) met DED criteria and 76 had passive-smoke exposure. Compared with children without DED, those diagnosed with DED had greater exposure measured in cigarettes per day (17.70 ± 14.19 versus 0.65 ± 2.55) and hours (10.00 ± 3.77 h versus 0.70 ± 2.38 h), p < 0.0001 for both. Cigarettes/day exposure was an important adjusted determinant; detailed clinical outcomes by exposure were not supplied.

document_sections.heading: 5.1.2.2. Tobacco and other ocular surface diseases
document_sections.content: A 2007 systematic review reported a strong association between smoking and thyroid eye disease despite variable study quality and size; odds ratios across its case-control studies ranged from 1.2 to 20.2, and non-smokers had more favorable outcomes in other included studies. Evidence on pterygium conflicts. A 2014 review of 24 studies involving over 95,000 participants found lower pterygium risk with smoking, particularly current smoking. A Singapore multiethnic population study reported OR 0.41; 95% CI 0.16–0.87 for current smoking. Other studies found no significant relationship, whereas a Southern Harbin population study of 5057 adults older than 50 years reported higher pterygium prevalence among smokers (OR 1.90, 95% CI 1.51–2.35; p = 0.001). Allergic rhino-conjunctivitis involves IgE-mediated nasal and ocular symptoms after allergen exposure. Smoke is described more as an irritant than an allergen. Evidence specifically linking smoking to ocular allergy is sparse: an analysis spanning Phase I to Phase III found a 2% reduction in tobacco use but no correlation with changing allergic rhino-conjunctivitis in either the 6–7 or 13-14-year age group (p = 0.23 and 0.62, respectively). An allergy-asthma chart review (n = 1037), including n = 580 with allergic rhino-conjunctivitis, found no association of smoking with IgE, skin-prick results, or eosinophils. In a US veteran study from 2010–2015 (n = 3,453,944), smoking, blepharitis, conjunctivitis, and allergy history were associated with chalazion in univariate and multivariable analyses; their contributions require further examination. Among n = 75 people with DED assessed for IgE from Schirmer strips, indoor-smoke exposure was associated with high IgE (OR 38.6, p = 0.008). Whether smoke directly induces that response or amplifies pre-existing immune reactivity remains uncertain.

document_sections.heading: 5.1.2.3. Smoking and the cornea
document_sections.content: A meta-analysis of 17 studies comprising 2077 smokers and 6429 non-smokers found greater central corneal thickness among smokers (mean difference of 3.3 μm, 95% CI + 0.9 to+5.7 μm, p = 0.007) and lower endothelial cell density (mean difference of 140 cells/mm2, 95% CI 30 to 250 cells/mm2, p = 0.01). Endothelial hexagonality and mean cell size did not differ significantly. The authors suggested possible endothelial effects but identified no corresponding clinical difference, such as increased need for endothelial surgery.

document_sections.heading: 5.1.3. Mechanisms
document_sections.content: In rabbit experiments, smoke from filtered and unfiltered cigarettes was applied to 12 healthy rabbits and 12 with hypercholesterolemia. Cells showed greater damage after unfiltered smoke and in hypercholesterolemic animals; differences appeared at 18 and 24 h, rather than in early cultures. Later work in mice and human corneal epithelial cells supported injury effects in intact and previously injured corneas. In another experiment, four adult female dogs and 32 pups, including 16 males, underwent intermittent smoke exposure for 105 days: endothelial cell density fell by 10% versus controls, and 524 proteins changed expression, including reductions in proteins associated with Descemet’s membrane. In humans, smoking a cigarette reduced tear breakup time and lipid-layer thickness within 5 min. Lipid oxidation and interactions with tear proteins are proposed contributors to instability; longer exposure may produce staining, inflammation, increased osmolarity, and possibly dryness or irritation. Toxins in heated tobacco products have damaged corneal epithelial cells. Further biochemical research could clarify these effects.

document_sections.heading: 5.1.4. Treatment implications
document_sections.content: Whether smoking definitively increases DED diagnosis remains uncertain, irrespective of whether diagnosis uses symptoms alone or includes signs. Its effects on tear film and epithelial cells are clearer and resemble DED findings; passive exposure may also contribute to this multifactorial condition. Clinicians should discuss possible ocular surface effects with patients because smoking is modifiable. Evidence that cessation improves ocular surface health is minimal or absent, so evaluating cessation interventions against DED outcomes warrants study. General health improvements from smoke-free policies might also benefit ocular surface health, but this has not been established.

document_sections.heading: 5.2. Cannabis
document_sections.content: This section reviews experimental ocular surface effects of cannabinoids and the limited clinical evidence concerning cannabis use.

document_sections.heading: 5.2.1. What is cannabis?
document_sections.content: Cannabis, or marijuana, comes from Cannabis sativa, indica, and rederalis plants and is used by more than 180 million people worldwide. It contains more than 540 naturally occurring compounds, including 110 cannabinoids. Δ9-tetrahydrocannabinol is its main psychotropic component, whereas cannabidiol is a principal non-psychoactive component. It is commonly smoked alone or mixed with tobacco.

document_sections.heading: 5.2.2. Cannabis and DED
document_sections.content: Early mouse work suggests that Δ9-tetrahydrocannabinol activation of lacrimal CB1 receptors can lower aqueous tear production. Experiments in murine, bovine, and human corneal epithelial cells implicate CB1, CB2, and GPR18 in wound healing and possible reductions in opacity and neovascularization. Natural and synthetic cannabinoids, including CBD, have shown anti-nociceptive and anti-inflammatory effects in mouse models of corneal hyperalgesia; therapeutic relevance remains unproven. Clinical research is sparse. A case-control comparison of 28 people with cannabinoid use disorder and 32 matched controls found lower endothelial cell density with long-term use (2900 ± 211 versus 3097 ± 214 cells/mm2, p < 0.01), but mechanisms are unclear. Another case-control study found higher basal tearing, intraocular pressure, and light sensitivity and worse dark adaptation among long-term users; values in both groups remained normal. Ocular surface effects of cannabinoids therefore remain uncertain. Better clinical studies are needed to test reported cannabis–DED associations, alongside experimental investigation of potential treatments for ocular surface injury.

document_sections.heading: 5.3. Other recreational drugs
document_sections.content: This section considers recreational substances in relation to ocular surface injury and disease.

document_sections.heading: 5.3.1. Recreational drugs and the eye
document_sections.content: Recreational drugs can alter systemic physiology, eye structures, and vision. This review focuses on the ocular surface rather than other ocular or visual effects. Because many drugs are illegal or toxic, available evidence often comes from case reports rather than controlled comparisons. The range of substances changes as new drugs and variants emerge; solvents and prescribed medicines can also be misused. Alcohol is widely consumed and may be treated separately from illegal recreational drugs. Eye-care professionals should recognize potential ocular effects of substance misuse.

document_sections.heading: 5.3.2. Recreational drugs and ocular surface disease
document_sections.content: Reported ocular surface effects differ across substances and routes of exposure; evidence for several drugs is limited to case reports or theoretical concerns.

document_sections.heading: 5.3.2.1. Methamphetamines
document_sections.content: Amphetamine-derived substances include 3,4Methylenedioxymethamphetamine (MDMA), also called ecstasy, E, or molly. They may be swallowed or snorted, can contain impurities, and even one dose can be fatal. Acute dehydration could affect the ocular surface, but the review identifies no documentation of that effect. Case reports associate methamphetamine with corneal ulcers that became infected and perforated. Its vasoconstrictive effects may lower ocular perfusion and blood flow. Intravenous methamphetamine has been linked in cases to conjunctivitis and episcleritis.

document_sections.heading: 5.3.2.2. Cocaine
document_sections.content: Cocaine may be snorted as powder or smoked as crack cocaine; it has anesthetic and stimulant effects and can produce serious systemic toxicity. Reports also suggest impaired smooth-pursuit eye movements in crack users. On the cornea, cocaine produces local anesthesia through the mechanism described in the cited research as sodium-channel blockade and prevention of acetylcholine binding. In a study of habitual cocaine snorters (n = 48), corneal sensitivity was lower than in heroin users (n = 22) and people without drug use (n = 30). Reduced sensitivity occurred in 26 cocaine users and no heroin users; 6 cocaine users had neurotrophic keratitis. Corneal epithelial defects and microbial keratitis have been reported after smoking or snorting cocaine. In a within-person study, 17 of 22 eyes showed reduced Schirmer tear production while under cocaine’s effects, with an average decrease of 16.52 ± 10.13 mm (range 1–38 mm), p = 0.0024. Crack smoking has been linked to corneal ulcers and epithelial defects. A review of 11 case reports found bilateral involvement in 63%, corneal infection in 83%, and marked visual impairment to hand movements only in 22%. Rubbing associated with drug-related behavior has been proposed as one cause of surface injury, not established as such. Case reports also link crack use to floppy eyelid syndrome. A report of direct topical cocaine application described severe corneal scarring in one eye and enucleation of the other after secondary angle-closure glaucoma.

document_sections.heading: 5.3.2.3. Opioids
document_sections.content: Natural and synthetic opioids, including morphine and heroin, are strongly addictive analgesic substances. Injection introduces additional blood-borne infection risks. Ocular surface effects are uncommon, but a case series of 3 people described hair loss, depigmentation, dermatitis, and DED, without a specified DED definition, after synthetic opioid MT-45 use. Reports concerning newborns of opioid-dependent mothers prescribed methadone during pregnancy found abnormal visual development: strabismus in 25%, described as 10-fold higher than in unaffected children, reduced visual acuity in 22%, and nystagmus in 11%. These findings concern visual development rather than an established ocular surface effect.

document_sections.heading: 5.3.2.4. Hallucinogens
document_sections.content: Lysergic Acid Diethylamide (LSD) changes visual perception and can cause anxiety or persistent perceptual effects. Whether it changes ocular surface measures is unknown. Direct ocular delivery might cause harm, and dry mouth raises only a possibility of ocular dryness; neither is established here as a demonstrated ocular surface outcome.

document_sections.heading: 5.3.2.5. Other recreational drugs
document_sections.content: Solvent misuse involves inhaling fumes from products such as aerosols, petrol, nail varnish, and glue. Ocular surface damage and symptoms are plausible given vapor exposure, but the review states that this question has not been directly studied.

document_sections.heading: 5.4. Alcohol
document_sections.content: Alcohol can affect the ocular surface through direct contact or oral consumption. Direct exposure, accidental or procedural, loosens corneal epithelium from Bowman’s membrane. Studies have identified drinking as a possible contributor to DED, although climate, psychological factors, and other confounders complicate interpretation; a Dutch study observed an association in women but not men. Heavy drinking may affect vision temporarily or contribute to chronic eye disease, potentially alongside poor nutrition. Reported findings link alcohol intake to tear-film deterioration and reduced tear volume. One study detected ethanol in tears alongside higher tear osmolarity and worse DED symptoms. Chronic consumption may produce vitamin A deficiency, with corneal and conjunctival keratinization that could induce or aggravate DED.

document_sections.heading: 5.5. Caffeine
document_sections.content: Caffeine (1,3,7-trimethylxanthine) is a psychostimulant in tea, coffee, and cacao; more than 70% of adults in modern Western societies consume it daily. At physiological concentrations, it antagonizes adenosine receptors. Two population-based cross-sectional studies associated regular intake with lower DED odds (OR 0.75 and 0.82, respectively, both p < 0.05), but other adjusted studies showed non-significant trends. One study that included caffeine from coffee, tea, cola, and energy drinks found no significant association with Women’s Health Study-defined DED; no dedicated study examined synthetic caffeine from energy drinks. Variation in DED definitions and self-reported intake limits these findings. Two prospective placebo-controlled crossover studies reported a rise in tear meniscus height (+0.08 mm; 95% CI +0.05 to +0.10 mm; p < 0.001) and Schirmer values (+2.96 mm; 95% CI +1.21 to +4.71 mm; p < 0.001) within the first 2 h after one dose of 5–7 mg/kg caffeine. During the ovulatory phase, an observational study associated intake with longer tear breakup time (r = 0.5, p = 0.02) and higher phenol red thread values (r = 0.5, p = 0.01). Mechanisms remain uncertain; stimulation of aqueous secretion through inhibition of 3′,5′-cyclic nucleotide phosphodiesterase has been hypothesized. Caffeine may protect the ocular surface, but larger, higher-quality prospective or randomized studies are needed before a preventive or therapeutic role in DED can be established.

document_sections.heading: 6. Conclusions and future directions
document_sections.content: Mental, physical, and social factors have been associated with DED symptoms and signs and with other ocular surface diseases. Most associations come from cross-sectional studies; longitudinal work should address confounding and DED’s multifactorial nature. Mechanistic and animal studies may help examine these relationships. Across populations, depression, anxiety, and stress relate more consistently to DED symptoms than signs, but mechanisms and optimal treatment of coexisting psychological disorders remain unclear. Sleep quality and duration are strongly associated with DED symptoms; whether this persists after accounting for psychosocial disorders requires study. Obesity has been linked to meibomian gland and eyelid abnormalities, potentially influenced by sleep apnea. Face-mask wear has emerged as a DED risk factor, particularly for evaporative DED and meibomian gland dysfunction. Sexual and reproductive issues have been linked to DED, but mechanisms and preventive or therapeutic approaches need investigation. Chronic pain conditions, particularly migraine, chronic pain syndrome, and fibromyalgia, commonly coexist with DED; the literature chiefly concerns symptoms, and heterogeneity calls for research into signs, aqueous deficient versus evaporative subtypes, and standardized pain measurement. Recreational-drug ocular effects depend on the substance and delivery route; evidence is often limited to case reports and series rather than case-control studies.
